Dash Help Magic Study

#### Your Turn  
On your turn, you can move a distance up to your Speed and take one action. You decide whether to move first or take your action first.  
The main actions you can take are listed in "Actions" earlier in "Playing the Game." A character's features and a monster's stat block also provide action options. "Movement and Position" later in "Playing the Game" gives the rules for movement.  
**Communicating.** You can communicate however you are able—through brief utterances and gestures—as you take your turn. Doing so uses neither your action nor your move.  
Extended communication, such as a detailed explanation of something or an attempt to persuade a foe, requires an action. The Influence action is the main way you try to influence a monster.  
**Interacting with Things.** You can interact with one object or feature of the environment for free, during either your move or action. For example, you could open a door during your move as you stride toward a foe.  
If you want to interact with a second object, you need to take the Utilize action. Some magic items and other special objects always require an action to use, as stated in their descriptions.  
The GM might require you to use an action for any of these activities when it needs special care or when it presents an unusual obstacle. For instance, the GM might require you to take the Utilize action to open a stuck door or turn a crank to lower a drawbridge.  
> **Playing on a Grid**
>
> If you play using a square grid and miniatures or other tokens, follow these rules.
>
> _Squares._ Each square represents 5 feet.
>
> _Speed._ Rather than moving foot by foot, move square by square on the grid, using your Speed in 5-foot segments. You can translate your Speed into squares by dividing it by 5. For example, a Speed of 30 feet translates into 6 squares. If you use a grid often, consider writing your Speed in squares on your character sheet.
>
> _Entering a Square._ To enter a square, you must have enough movement left to pay for entering. It costs 1 square of movement to enter an unoccupied square that's adjacent to your space (orthogonally or diagonally adjacent). A square of Difficult Terrain costs 2 squares to enter. Other effects might make a square cost even more.
>
> _Corners._ Diagonal movement can't cross the corner of a wall, a large tree, or another terrain feature that fills its space.
>
> _Ranges._ To determine the range on a grid between two things—whether creatures or objects—count squares from a square adjacent to one of them and stop counting in the space of the other one. Count by the shortest route.  
_Doing Nothing on Your Turn._ You can forgo moving, taking an action, or doing anything at all on your turn. If you can't decide what to do, consider taking the defensive Dodge action or the Ready action to delay acting.

### Bonus Actions  
Various class features, spells, and other abilities let you take an additional action on your turn called a Bonus Action. The Cunning Action feature, for example, allows a Rogue to take a Bonus Action. You can take a Bonus Action only when a special ability, a spell, or another feature of the game states that you can do something as a Bonus Action. You otherwise don't have a Bonus Action to take.  
You can take only one Bonus Action on your turn, so you must choose which Bonus Action to use if you have more than one available.  
You choose when to take a Bonus Action during your turn unless the Bonus Action's timing is specified. Anything that deprives you of your ability to take actions also prevents you from taking a Bonus Action.

#### Simultaneous Effects  
If two or more things happen at the same time on a turn, the person at the game table—player or GM—whose turn it is decides the order in which those things happen. For example, if two effects occur at the start of a player character's turn, the player decides which of the effects happens first.

### Reactions  
Certain special abilities, spells, and situations allow you to take a special action called a Reaction. A Reaction is an instant response to a trigger of some kind, which can occur on your turn or on someone else's. The Opportunity Attack, described later in "Playing the Game," is the most common type of Reaction.  
When you take a Reaction, you can't take another one until the start of your next turn. If the reaction interrupts another creature's turn, that creature can continue its turn right after the Reaction.  
In terms of timing, a Reaction takes place immediately after its trigger unless the Reaction's description says otherwise.

#### Disengage [Action]  
If you take the Disengage action, your movement doesn't provoke Opportunity Attacks for the rest of the current turn.

# Delaying Your Turn

**No, you cannot delay your turn to act later in the round.** The SRD 5.2.1 rules do not include a "Delay" action or any mechanism for voluntarily pushing your turn to a later point in the initiative order.

What you **can** do is the **Ready action**, which is mentioned in the context as a way to "delay acting." However, this is not the same as delaying your turn. When you take the Ready action, you use your action on your turn to prepare a response that triggers later (using your Reaction). You still act on your normal initiative turn — you're simply holding your action to respond to a specific trigger, rather than acting later in the initiative order.

The context also notes that you can **forgo moving, taking an action, or doing anything at all on your turn**, but this means you simply do nothing — you don't get to act at a later initiative position.

In summary, there is no rule in SRD 5.2.1 that allows you to change your place in the initiative order or postpone your entire turn.

#### Action On your turn, you can take one action. Choose which action to take from those below or from the special actions provided by your features. _See also_ "Playing the Game" ("Actions"). These actions are defined elsewhere in this glossary:
Attack Dodge Influence Search
Dash Help Magic Study
Disengage Hide Ready Utilize

#### Your Turn  
On your turn, you can move a distance up to your Speed and take one action. You decide whether to move first or take your action first.  
The main actions you can take are listed in "Actions" earlier in "Playing the Game." A character's features and a monster's stat block also provide action options. "Movement and Position" later in "Playing the Game" gives the rules for movement.  
**Communicating.** You can communicate however you are able—through brief utterances and gestures—as you take your turn. Doing so uses neither your action nor your move.  
Extended communication, such as a detailed explanation of something or an attempt to persuade a foe, requires an action. The Influence action is the main way you try to influence a monster.  
**Interacting with Things.** You can interact with one object or feature of the environment for free, during either your move or action. For example, you could open a door during your move as you stride toward a foe.  
If you want to interact with a second object, you need to take the Utilize action. Some magic items and other special objects always require an action to use, as stated in their descriptions.  
The GM might require you to use an action for any of these activities when it needs special care or when it presents an unusual obstacle. For instance, the GM might require you to take the Utilize action to open a stuck door or turn a crank to lower a drawbridge.  
> **Playing on a Grid**
>
> If you play using a square grid and miniatures or other tokens, follow these rules.
>
> _Squares._ Each square represents 5 feet.
>
> _Speed._ Rather than moving foot by foot, move square by square on the grid, using your Speed in 5-foot segments. You can translate your Speed into squares by dividing it by 5. For example, a Speed of 30 feet translates into 6 squares. If you use a grid often, consider writing your Speed in squares on your character sheet.
>
> _Entering a Square._ To enter a square, you must have enough movement left to pay for entering. It costs 1 square of movement to enter an unoccupied square that's adjacent to your space (orthogonally or diagonally adjacent). A square of Difficult Terrain costs 2 squares to enter. Other effects might make a square cost even more.
>
> _Corners._ Diagonal movement can't cross the corner of a wall, a large tree, or another terrain feature that fills its space.
>
> _Ranges._ To determine the range on a grid between two things—whether creatures or objects—count squares from a square adjacent to one of them and stop counting in the space of the other one. Count by the shortest route.  
_Doing Nothing on Your Turn._ You can forgo moving, taking an action, or doing anything at all on your turn. If you can't decide what to do, consider taking the defensive Dodge action or the Ready action to delay acting.

### Bonus Actions  
Various class features, spells, and other abilities let you take an additional action on your turn called a Bonus Action. The Cunning Action feature, for example, allows a Rogue to take a Bonus Action. You can take a Bonus Action only when a special ability, a spell, or another feature of the game states that you can do something as a Bonus Action. You otherwise don't have a Bonus Action to take.  
You can take only one Bonus Action on your turn, so you must choose which Bonus Action to use if you have more than one available.  
You choose when to take a Bonus Action during your turn unless the Bonus Action's timing is specified. Anything that deprives you of your ability to take actions also prevents you from taking a Bonus Action.

#### Simultaneous Effects  
If two or more things happen at the same time on a turn, the person at the game table—player or GM—whose turn it is decides the order in which those things happen. For example, if two effects occur at the start of a player character's turn, the player decides which of the effects happens first.

### Reactions  
Certain special abilities, spells, and situations allow you to take a special action called a Reaction. A Reaction is an instant response to a trigger of some kind, which can occur on your turn or on someone else's. The Opportunity Attack, described later in "Playing the Game," is the most common type of Reaction.  
When you take a Reaction, you can't take another one until the start of your next turn. If the reaction interrupts another creature's turn, that creature can continue its turn right after the Reaction.  
In terms of timing, a Reaction takes place immediately after its trigger unless the Reaction's description says otherwise.

#### Disengage [Action]  
If you take the Disengage action, your movement doesn't provoke Opportunity Attacks for the rest of the current turn.

retrieved_context.text:
#### Surprise  
If a creature is caught unawares by the start of combat, that creature is surprised, which causes it to have Disadvantage on its Initiative roll. _See also_ "Playing the Game" ("Combat").

#### Initiative  
Initiative determines the order of turns during combat. When combat starts, every participant rolls Initiative; they make a Dexterity check that determines their place in the Initiative order. The GM rolls for monsters. For a group of identical creatures, the GM makes a single roll, so each member of the group has the same Initiative.  
**Surprise.** If a combatant is surprised by combat starting, that combatant has Disadvantage on their Initiative roll. For example, if an ambusher starts combat while hidden from a foe who is unaware that combat is starting, that foe is surprised.  
**Initiative Order.** A combatant's check total is called their Initiative count, or Initiative for short. The GM ranks the combatants, from highest to lowest Initiative. This is the order in which they act during each round. The Initiative order remains the same from round to round.  
**Ties.** If a tie occurs, the GM decides the order among tied monsters, and the players decide the order among tied characters. The GM decides the order if the tie is between a monster and a player character.

### Reactions  
If the monster has Reaction options, those are listed in this section along with their triggers. See "Playing the Game" for details on Reactions.

#### Actions  
<hr>  
**_Shock._** _Melee Attack Roll:_ +4, reach 5 ft. _Hit:_ 11 (2d8 + 2) Lightning damage.

#### Level 14: Devious Strikes  
You've practiced new ways to use your Sneak Attack deviously. The following effects are now among your Cunning Strike options.  
_Daze (Cost: 2d6)._ The target must succeed on a Constitution saving throw, or on its next turn, it can do only one of the following: move or take an action or a Bonus Action.  
_Knock Out (Cost: 6d6)._ The target must succeed on a Constitution saving throw, or it has the Unconscious condition for 1 minute or until it takes any damage. The Unconscious target repeats the save at the end of each of its turns, ending the effect on itself on a success.  
_Obscure (Cost: 3d6)._ The target must succeed on a Dexterity saving throw, or it has the Blinded condition until the end of its next turn.

**Surprise** is a condition that occurs when a creature is caught unawares at the start of combat. Here's how it works:

1. **Determination:** If a combatant is surprised by the start of combat (e.g., an ambusher attacks while hidden from a foe who is unaware combat is beginning), that combatant is **surprised**.

2. **Effect on Initiative:** A surprised creature has **Disadvantage on its Initiative roll** (the Dexterity check made to determine turn order).

3. **No further mechanical effect specified:** The SRD 5.2.1 text only explicitly states the Disadvantage on Initiative. It does not, within the provided context, mention any additional restrictions such as being unable to move or take actions on the first turn (which is a common point of confusion carried over from older editions).

In summary, per the SRD 5.2.1, **Surprise = Disadvantage on Initiative**. The GM determines who is surprised based on the circumstances of combat's onset (e.g., hidden ambushers vs. unaware foes).

**Answer:** Yes, the Druid can use Misty Step to break the grapple while Wild‑Shaped as a wolf.

**Reasoning (SRD 5.2.1):**

1. **Wild Shape Mechanics** – While in a Wild Shape form, the Druid retains their own ability scores, class features, and proficiencies (including spellcasting ability and spell slots) but cannot cast spells directly from the form.  
2. **Beast Spells (Level 18)** – This class feature explicitly states: *“While using Wild Shape, you can cast spells in Beast form, except for any spell that has a Material component with a cost specified or that consumes its Material component.”* Misty Step has no material component, so it is allowed.  
3. **Movement and Actions** – The wolf’s stat block (a typical Small‑to‑Medium beast) provides a movement speed (e.g., 30 ft. land speed) and any natural abilities (such as a bite or pounce). The Druid retains the ability to take actions that their form can physically perform, including moving away from a grappling source.  
4. **Breaking a Grapple** – To end a grapple, a creature must either succeed on a Strength (Athletics) check (Escape) or move out of the grappler’s reach. Since the wolf can move its full speed, the Druid can simply move away, ending the grapple.  
5. **Misty Step** – As a spell that teleports the caster 60 ft. to an unoccupied space, it is a valid action for the Druid while in Wild Shape (per Beast Spells) and does not require material components. Casting it while grappling will instantly place the Druid outside the grappler’s reach, thereby breaking the grapple.

Therefore, the Druid can indeed use Misty Step to escape a grapple while Wild‑Shaped as a wolf.  

**Conclusion:** **Yes**.

When a creature with Magic Resistance is targeted by a Sorcerer who uses Heightened Spell on a save‑based spell, the net effect on the creature's saving throw is as follows:

1. **Magic Resistance** gives the creature **Advantage** on the saving throw, meaning its roll is treated as if it had two d20s and the higher result is used.
2. **Heightened Spell** (spending 2 Sorcery Points) imposes **Disadvantage** on the saving throw for the chosen target, meaning the creature rolls two d20s and takes the lower result.

When Advantage and Disadvantage are applied to the same roll, they cancel each other out. Therefore, the two effects negate one another, leaving the creature's saving throw **unchanged** from its normal state (i.e., it retains its standard roll without any additional benefit or penalty). 

In summary, the net effect on the save is **zero**; the creature's saving throw proceeds as normal, unaffected by either feature.

You know how to strike subtly and exploit a foe's distraction. Once per turn, you can deal an extra 1d6 damage to one creature you hit with an attack roll if you have Advantage on the roll and the attack uses a Finesse or a Ranged weapon. The extra damage's type is the same as the weapon's type.  
You don't need Advantage on the attack roll if at least one of your allies is within 5 feet of the target, the ally doesn't have the Incapacitated condition, and you don't have Disadvantage on the attack roll. The extra damage increases as you gain Rogue levels, as shown in the Sneak Attack column of the Rogue Features table.

### Rogue Class Features As a Rogue, you gain the following class features when you reach the specified Rogue levels. These features are listed in the Rogue Features table. **Rogue Features**
Level Proficiency Bonus Class Features Sneak Attack
1 +2 Expertise, Sneak Attack, Thieves' Cant, Weapon Mastery 1d6
2 +2 Cunning Action 1d6
3 +2 Rogue Subclass, Steady Aim 2d6
4 +2 Ability Score Improvement 2d6

20 +6 Stroke of Luck 10d6

## Rogue **Core Rogue Traits**
Primary Ability Dexterity
Hit Point Die D8 per Rogue level
Saving Throw Proficiencies Dexterity and Intelligence
Skill Proficiencies Choose 4: Acrobatics, Athletics, Deception, Insight, Intimidation, Investigation, Perception, Persuasion, Sleight of Hand, or Stealth
Weapon Proficiencies Simple weapons and Martial weapons that have the Finesse or Light property
Tool Proficiencies Thieves' Tools
Armor Training Light armor
Starting Equipment Choose A or B: (A) Leather Armor, 2 Daggers, Shortsword, Shortbow, 20 Arrows, Quiver, Thieves' Tools, Burglar's Pack, and 8 GP; or (B) 100 GP

#### Level 5: Cunning Strike  
You've developed cunning ways to use your Sneak Attack. When you deal Sneak Attack damage, you can add one of the following Cunning Strike effects. Each effect has a die cost, which is the number of Sneak Attack damage dice you must forgo to add the effect. You remove the die before rolling, and the effect occurs immediately after the attack's damage is dealt. For example, if you add the Poison effect, remove 1d6 from the Sneak Attack's damage before rolling.  
If a Cunning Strike effect requires a saving throw, the DC equals 8 plus your Dexterity modifier and Proficiency Bonus.  
_Poison (Cost: 1d6)._ You add a toxin to your strike, forcing the target to make a Constitution saving throw. On a failed save, the target has the Poisoned condition for 1 minute. At the end of each of its turns, the Poisoned target repeats the save, ending the effect on itself on a success.  
To use this effect, you must have a Poisoner's Kit on your person.  
_Trip (Cost: 1d6)._ If the target is Large or smaller, it must succeed on a Dexterity saving throw or have the Prone condition.  
_Withdraw (Cost: 1d6)._ Immediately after the attack, you move up to half your Speed without provoking Opportunity Attacks.

#### Actions  
<hr>  
**_Greataxe._** _Melee Attack Roll:_ +5, reach 5 ft. _Hit:_ 9 (1d12 + 3) Slashing damage.

#### Level 9: Supreme Sneak  
You gain the following Cunning Strike option.  
_Stealth Attack (Cost: 1d6)._ If you have the Hide action's Invisible condition, this attack doesn't end that condition on you if you end the turn behind Three-Quarters Cover or Total Cover.

#### Level 3: Improved Critical  
Your attack rolls with weapons and Unarmed Strikes can score a Critical Hit on a roll of 19 or 20 on the d20.

Your attack rolls with weapons and Unarmed Strikes can now score a Critical Hit on a roll of 18–20 on the d20.

#### Vicious Weapon  
_Weapon (Any Simple or Martial), Rare_  
This magic weapon deals an extra 2d6 damage to any creature it hits. This extra damage is of the same type as the weapon's normal damage.

### Critical Hits  
When you score a Critical Hit, you deal extra damage. Roll the attack's damage dice twice, add them together, and add any relevant modifiers as normal. For example, if you score a Critical Hit with a Dagger, roll 2d4 for the damage rather than 1d4, and add your relevant ability modifier. If the attack involves other damage dice, such as from the Rogue's Sneak Attack feature, you also roll those dice twice.

_Level 2 Illusion (Bard, Cleric, Ranger)_  
**Casting Time:** Action or Ritual
**Range:** 120 feet
**Components:** V, S
**Duration:** Concentration, up to 10 minutes  
For the duration, no sound can be created within or pass through a 20-foot-radius Sphere centered on a point you choose within range. Casting a spell that includes a Verbal component is impossible there.

#### Imprisonment  
_Level 9 Abjuration (Warlock, Wizard)_  
**Casting Time:** 1 minute
**Range:** 30 feet
**Components:** V, S, M (a statuette of the target worth 5,000+ GP)
**Duration:** Until dispelled  
You create a magical restraint to hold a creature that you can see within range. The target must make a Wisdom saving throw. #### Opportunity Attacks  
You can make an Opportunity Attack when a creature that you can see leaves your reach using its action, its Bonus Action, its Reaction, or one of its speeds. To make the Opportunity Attack, take a Reaction to make one melee attack with a weapon or an Unarmed Strike against the provoking creature. The attack occurs right before the creature leaves your reach. _See also_ "Playing the Game" ("Combat").

#### Opportunity Attacks  
Combatants watch for enemies to drop their guard. If you move heedlessly past your foes, you put yourself in danger by provoking an Opportunity Attack.  
_Avoiding Opportunity Attacks._ You can avoid provoking an Opportunity Attack by taking the Disengage action. You also don't provoke an Opportunity Attack when you Teleport or when you are moved without using your movement, action, Bonus Action, or Reaction. For example, you don't provoke an Opportunity Attack if an explosion hurls you out of a foe's reach or if you fall past an enemy.  
_Making an Opportunity Attack._ You can make an Opportunity Attack when a creature that you can see leaves your reach. To make the attack, take a Reaction to make one melee attack with a weapon or an Unarmed Strike against that creature. The attack occurs right before it leaves your reach.

# Topple on an Opportunity Attack with a Glaive vs. Magic Resistance

**Yes, Topple can be applied, and Magic Resistance does not help the target.**

Here's the breakdown:

1. **Topple requires a Flurry of Blows attack.** The Topple option from Open Hand Technique (Level 3: Open Hand Technique) triggers "whenever you hit a creature with an attack granted by your Flurry of Blows." Flurry of Blows is a Monk feature that grants bonus unarmed strikes — it does **not** grant Opportunity Attacks. An Opportunity Attack is a Reaction-based melee attack, not a Flurry of Blows attack.

2. **Therefore, Topple cannot be applied to an Opportunity Attack.** The trigger for Topple is specifically an attack from Flurry of Blows, and an Opportunity Attack is not one of those attacks. The weapon used (Glaive or otherwise) is irrelevant — the source of the attack matters, not the weapon.

3. **Magic Resistance is moot here.** Magic Resistance (advantage on saving throws against spells and other magical effects) would only matter if Topple were a spell or magical effect. Topple from Open Hand Technique is a class feature that imposes a Dexterity saving throw. Whether it counts as a "magical effect" for the purposes of Magic Resistance is debatable, but since the attack doesn't qualify for Topple in the first place, this point is irrelevant.

**In short:** Topple does not work on an Opportunity Attack because the attack must come from Flurry of Blows, not a Reaction-based Opportunity Attack. The Glaive and Magic Resistance are red herrings in this scenario.

**What the rules say**

- **Size and reach** – A *Large* creature has a space of 10 ft × 10 ft and a natural reach of 10 ft (the distance from its body to the edge of its space).  
- **Grapple rules (PHB p. 195)** – To attempt a grapple, a creature must be able to reach the target. The attacker must make a successful *grapple check* (Strength (Athletics) check) and the target must be within the attacker’s reach. If the check succeeds, the target is **grappled** and the grappler can later use the *Shove* action to move the target.

**Applying this to the scenario**

1. **Reach check** – The Medium Paladin’s natural reach is 5 ft (the distance from his body to the edge of his 5 ft × 5 ft space). The Large dragon’s space extends 5 ft beyond its body, so the closest point of the dragon to the Paladin is **5 ft away**.  
2. **Can the Paladin reach?** – Yes. The Paladin’s reach (5 ft) is sufficient to reach any point on the dragon’s body that is within 5 ft of the dragon’s space edge. Because the dragon is flying, the Paladin must be able to move into the dragon’s space (or at least within 5 ft of it) to attempt the grapple. If the Paladin can position himself so that the distance to the dragon is ≤ 5 ft, the grapple attempt proceeds.  
3. **Grapple check** – The Paladin makes a Strength (Athletics) check against the dragon’s *grapple DC* (which is the dragon’s Strength (Athletics) score plus any relevant modifiers). If the check succeeds, the dragon becomes **grappled**.  
4. **Effect of being grappled while flying** – Once grappled, the dragon must end its turn **within the grappler’s space** (or at least within 5 ft of the grappler) and cannot move freely. The dragon can attempt to break the grapple on its turn with a *grapple check* of its own (Strength (Athletics) vs. the Paladin’s). If the dragon fails to break the grapple, it remains restrained and the Paladin can later use the *Shove* action to move the dragon (subject to the usual shove rules).  

**Conclusion**

A Medium Paladin can grapple a Large dragon while it is flying **provided the Paladin can get within 5 ft of the dragon** (i.e., within the dragon’s space or within reach). If the Paladin succeeds on the grapple check, the dragon becomes grappled, is restrained, and must move with the Paladin until it breaks the grapple. No special size‑based penalty beyond the normal reach requirement applies.  

**Key points**

- Reach requirement: Paladin must be ≤ 5 ft from the dragon.  
- Grapple succeeds on a successful Strength (Athletics) check.  
- Grappled dragon is restrained and must end its turn within the grappler’s space; it can attempt to break the grapple each turn.  

Thus, the scenario is fully governed by the standard grapple rules; the dragon’s Large size and flying status do not alter the mechanics beyond the reach check.

**What the rules say**

- **Size and reach** – A *Large* creature has a space of 10 ft × 10 ft and a natural reach of 10 ft (the distance from its body to the edge of its space).  
- **Grapple rules (PHB p. 195)** – To attempt a grapple, a creature must be able to reach the target. The attacker must make a successful *grapple check* (Strength (Athletics) check) and the target must be within the attacker’s reach. If the check succeeds, the target is **grappled** and the grappler can later use the *Shove* action to move the target.

**Applying this to the scenario**

1. **Reach check** – The Medium Paladin’s natural reach is 5 ft (the distance from his body to the edge of his 5 ft × 5 ft space). The Large dragon’s space extends 5 ft beyond its body, so the closest point of the dragon to the Paladin is **5 ft away**.  
2. **Can the Paladin reach?** – Yes. The Paladin’s reach (5 ft) is sufficient to reach any point on the dragon’s body that is within 5 ft of the dragon’s space edge. Because the dragon is flying, the Paladin must be able to move into the dragon’s space (or at least within 5 ft of it) to attempt the grapple. If the Paladin can position himself so that the distance to the dragon is ≤ 5 ft, the grapple attempt proceeds.  
3. **Grapple check** – The Paladin makes a Strength (Athletics) check against the dragon’s *grapple DC* (which is the dragon’s Strength (Athletics) score plus any relevant modifiers). If the check succeeds, the dragon becomes **grappled**.  
4. **Effect of being grappled while flying** – Once grappled, the dragon must end its turn **within the grappler’s space** (or at least within 5 ft of the grappler) and cannot move freely. The dragon can attempt to break the grapple on its turn with a *grapple check* of its own (Strength (Athletics) vs. the Paladin’s). If the dragon fails to break the grapple, it remains restrained and the Paladin can later use the *Shove* action to move the dragon (subject to the usual shove rules).  

**Conclusion**

A Medium Paladin can grapple a Large dragon while it is flying **provided the Paladin can get within 5 ft of the dragon** (i.e., within the dragon’s space or within reach). If the Paladin succeeds on the grapple check, the dragon becomes grappled, is restrained, and must move with the Paladin until it breaks the grapple. No special size‑based penalty beyond the normal reach requirement applies.  

**Key points**

- Reach requirement: Paladin must be ≤ 5 ft from the dragon.  
- Grapple succeeds on a successful Strength (Athletics) check.  
- Grappled dragon is restrained and must end its turn within the grappler’s space; it can attempt to break the grapple each turn.  

Thus, the scenario is fully governed by the standard grapple rules; the dragon’s Large size and flying status do not alter the mechanics beyond the reach check.

**Answer:** Yes, the creature that is pushed into the Spirit Guardians emanation by Thunderwave will take the Spirit Guardians damage.

**Reasoning:**  
- **Spirit Guardians** creates a 15‑foot emanation centered on the caster. Any creature that **enters** this emanation (or ends its turn there) must make a Wisdom saving throw; on a failure it takes radiant (or necrotic) damage.  
- **Thunderwave** is an instantaneous spell that pushes each creature in a 15‑foot cube 10 feet away from the caster. The spell’s description does not grant any special exception to the effects of other spells that might be present in the area.  
- When a creature is pushed by Thunderwave into the Spirit Guardians emanation, that movement **places the creature within the emanation**. Because the creature has not yet made the Wisdom saving throw for that turn (the saving throw is triggered “whenever a creature enters the Emanation or ends its turn there”), the creature must now make the saving throw and take the appropriate damage (3d8 radiant or necrotic, depending on the caster’s alignment).  

Thus, the Spirit Guardians damage applies to any creature that ends its turn in the emanation, including one that was just pushed there by Thunderwave.  

**Conclusion:** The pushed creature will suffer the Spirit Guardians damage as normal.

#### Pact of the Tome  
Stitching together strands of shadow, you conjure forth a book in your hand at the end of a Short or Long Rest. This _Book of Shadows_ (you determine its appearance) contains eldritch magic that only you can access, granting you the benefits below. The book disappears if you conjure another book with this feature or if you die.  
_Cantrips and Rituals._ When the book appears, choose three cantrips, and choose two level 1 spells that have the Ritual tag. As a Bonus Action, you can conjure a pact weapon in your hand—a Simple or Martial Melee weapon of your choice with which you bond—or create a bond with a magic weapon you touch; you can't bond with a magic weapon if someone else is attuned to it or another Warlock is bonded with it. Until the bond ends, you have proficiency with the weapon, and you can use it as a Spellcasting Focus.  
Whenever you attack with the bonded weapon, you can use your Charisma modifier for the attack and damage rolls instead of using Strength or Dexterity; and you can cause the weapon to deal Necrotic, Psychic, or Radiant damage or its normal damage type.

plus another 1d8 per level of the spell slot, and you can give the target the Prone condition if it is Huge or smaller.

# Grappling a Flying Large Dragon

## The Grapple Itself

A Medium Paladin can grapple a Large creature — the rules allow grappling a creature no more than one size larger than you. So a Medium character grappling a Large dragon is legal.

The Paladin makes a **Contested Check**: their Athletics vs. the dragon's Athletics or Acrobatics. The Young Bronze Dragon has STR +5 and proficiency +3, giving it **+8 to Athletics** (and +3 to Acrobatics). The Paladin would need to beat that.

## What Happens to the Dragon's Flight

This is where the SRD 5.2.1 context is **incomplete**. The rules don't explicitly state what happens when a flying creature is grappled. However, the general principles are:

- **Grappled condition** reduces the target's speed to 0. If the dragon's fly speed is reduced to 0, it **cannot fly** and would begin to fall.
- The dragon could attempt to **break the grapple** on its turn (contested check) or use **Repulsion Breath** (Strength save DC 19) to push the Paladin away and end the grapple.
- The dragon's **Shapechange** ability (at will, no concentration) could also be used to transform into a form that might escape or change the dynamic.

## What Happens to the Paladin

If the dragon falls, the Paladin falls too — they're grappling the dragon and would descend together, taking **falling damage** (1d6 per 10 feet fallen) unless the Paladin has a way to mitigate it (e.g., *feather fall*, a fly speed, or similar).

## Summary

If the Paladin succeeds on the grapple, the dragon's speed becomes 0, which would **ground the flying dragon** and cause both to fall. The dragon has strong options to escape (breaking the grapple, Repulsion Breath, or Shapechange), but if it can't, both plummet. The SRD doesn't provide a specific rule for this exact scenario, so the DM would need to adjudicate based on the general grappled condition and falling rules.

The rules for Bonus Actions state that a character can take one Bonus Action during their turn, in addition to their regular action and any reactions. **Answer:**  
No, the Cleave feature does **not** trigger from the Frenzy attack, and it cannot trigger twice in a single turn.

**Reasoning:**  

1. **Cleave (Weapon Mastery, Level 1)** – The Cleave mastery property allows you to make a second attack **only when you reduce a creature to 0 hit points with a melee attack**. The second attack must be made with the same weapon and against a different target within 5 feet of the original target.  

2. **Frenzy (Level 3 Barbarian feature)** – While Frenzy is active, if you use Reckless Attack, the *first* Strength‑based attack you make on your turn deals extra damage (determined by your Rage Damage bonus). This extra damage is **not** an additional attack; it is a damage bonus applied to the single attack roll.  

3. **Interaction** – Because the Frenzy attack is a single attack that merely adds extra damage, it does **not** reduce any creature to 0 hit points (unless the base attack already does so). Since the trigger for Cleave is “reducing a creature to 0 hit points,” the Frenzy attack does not satisfy this condition. Consequently, Cleave cannot be triggered by the Frenzy attack.  

4. **Multiple triggers in one turn** – Cleave can only be triggered once per turn, and it requires the specific condition of dropping a foe to 0 HP. Since the Frenzy attack does not meet that condition, there is no possibility for Cleave to trigger twice in the same turn.  

**Conclusion:** The Cleave mastery does not activate from a Frenzy‑enhanced attack, and it cannot trigger more than once per turn under the given circumstances.  

*(Source: SRD 5.2.1 – Cleave (Weapon Mastery) and Frenzy (Barbarian Level 3) descriptions.)*

#### Level 3: Frenzy  
If you use Reckless Attack while your Rage is active, you deal extra damage to the first target you hit on your turn with a Strength-based attack. #### Traits

**_Bloodied Frenzy._** While Bloodied, the berserker has Advantage on attack rolls and saving throws.

#### Berserker Axe  
_Weapon (Battleaxe, Greataxe, or Halberd), Rare (Requires Attunement)_  
You gain a +1 bonus to attack rolls and damage rolls made with this magic weapon. In addition, while you are attuned to this weapon, your Hit Point maximum increases by 1 for each level you have attained.  
_Curse._ This weapon is cursed, and becoming attuned to it extends the curse to you. As long as you remain cursed, you are unwilling to part with the weapon, keeping it within reach at all times. You also have Disadvantage on attack rolls with weapons other than this one.  
Whenever another creature damages you while the weapon is in your possession, you must succeed on a DC 15 Wisdom saving throw or go berserk. This berserk state ends when you start your turn and there are no creatures within 60 feet of you that you can see or hear.  
While berserk, you regard the creature nearest to you that you can see or hear as your enemy. If there are multiple possible creatures, choose one at random. On each of your turns, you must move as close to the creature as possible and take the Attack action, targeting the creature. If you're unable to get close enough to the creature to attack it with the weapon, your turn ends after you've used up all your available movement. If the creature dies or can no longer be seen or heard by you, the next nearest creature that you can see or hear becomes your new target.

#### Level 1: Weapon Mastery

_Sundering Blow._ Before the start of your next turn, the next attack roll made by another creature against the target gains a +5 bonus to the roll. An attack roll can gain only one Sundering Blow bonus.

#### Level 2: Reckless Attack  
You can throw aside all concern for defense to attack with increased ferocity. When you make your first attack roll on your turn, you can decide to attack recklessly. Doing so gives you Advantage on attack rolls using Strength until the start of your next turn, but attack rolls against you have Advantage during that time.

#### Level 3: Frenzy  
If you use Reckless Attack while your Rage is active, you deal extra damage to the first target you hit on your turn with a Strength-based attack. <hr>  
**_Bloodied Frenzy._** While Bloodied, the berserker has Advantage on attack rolls and saving throws.

#### Berserker Axe  
_Weapon (Battleaxe, Greataxe, or Halberd), Rare (Requires Attunement)_  
You gain a +1 bonus to attack rolls and damage rolls made with this magic weapon. In addition, while you are attuned to this weapon, your Hit Point maximum increases by 1 for each level you have attained.  
_Curse._ This weapon is cursed, and becoming attuned to it extends the curse to you. As long as you remain cursed, you are unwilling to part with the weapon, keeping it within reach at all times. You also have Disadvantage on attack rolls with weapons other than this one.  
Whenever another creature damages you while the weapon is in your possession, you must succeed on a DC 15 Wisdom saving throw or go berserk. This berserk state ends when you start your turn and there are no creatures within 60 feet of you that you can see or hear.  
While berserk, you regard the creature nearest to you that you can see or hear as your enemy. If there are multiple possible creatures, choose one at random. On each of your turns, you must move as close to the creature as possible and take the Attack action, targeting the creature. If you're unable to get close enough to the creature to attack it with the weapon, your turn ends after you've used up all your available movement. If the creature dies or can no longer be seen or heard by you, the next nearest creature that you can see or hear becomes your new target.

_Staggering Blow._ The target has Disadvantage on the next saving throw it makes, and it can't make Opportunity Attacks until the start of your next turn.  
_Sundering Blow._ Before the start of your next turn, the next attack roll made by another creature against the target gains a +5 bonus to the roll. An attack roll can gain only one Sundering Blow bonus.

You can throw aside all concern for defense to attack with increased ferocity. When you make your first attack roll on your turn, you can decide to attack recklessly. Doing so gives you Advantage on attack rolls using Strength until the start of your next turn, but attack rolls against you have Advantage during that time.

answer:
# Cleave and Frenzy

## Does Cleave trigger from the Frenzy attack?

**Yes.** The Frenzy feature states that when you use Reckless Attack while Raging, you deal extra damage to **the first target you hit on your turn** with a Strength-based attack. Cleave's mastery property triggers when you hit a creature with a melee attack using a weapon with the Cleave property — it allows you to make an additional melee attack against a second creature within 5 feet of the first target, using the same weapon. Since Cleave triggers off a hit, and the Frenzy bonus damage applies to the first hit on your turn, the Cleave attack (being a separate attack that also hits) would **not** benefit from the Frenzy extra damage, because it is not the *first* hit. However, Cleave itself **does trigger** from the Frenzy attack — the Frenzy attack is still a melee weapon attack, so if it hits, Cleave's condition is met and you can make the bonus attack against a second creature.

## Can Cleave trigger twice in a turn?

**No, not from Frenzy alone.** Cleave triggers when you hit a creature with a melee attack using a Cleave weapon. In a standard turn with Frenzy, you get your normal Attack action attacks plus one Frenzy bonus attack. Cleave can only trigger **once per attack that hits** — but the key limitation is that Cleave's additional attack is a **bonus action** (or a free extra attack granted by the mastery property on that specific hit). The SRD does not explicitly limit Cleave to once per turn, but since you only get a limited number of attacks, Cleave can only trigger on each individual hit. With Frenzy, if you have Extra Attack (Level 5), you could potentially trigger Cleave on multiple hits across your turn — **once per qualifying hit**, not twice from a single attack. Each attack that hits can trigger Cleave independently, so if you land multiple attacks in a turn, each could theoretically trigger Cleave.

**In short:** Cleave triggers from the Frenzy attack's hit, but the Frenzy bonus damage only applies to the first hit of the turn. Cleave can trigger on each separate attack that hits during your turn, not just once.

According to the SRD 5.2.1, a **Stunned** creature **cannot speak** and **cannot cast spells**.

The **Stunned** condition includes the **Incapacitated** condition. While the provided text does not explicitly define "Incapacitated," in the standard D&D 5e rules (as reflected in the SRD), the **Incapacitated** condition means a creature **can’t take actions or reactions**.

- **Can a Stunned creature speak?** **No.**
- **Can a Stunned creature cast spells?** **No.**

   - Grants Disadvantage on attack rolls against targets other than the grappler.

answer:
# Restrained AND Grappled — Do Effects Stack?

**No, identical effects do not stack, but the two conditions are not identical — they have distinct effects, and a creature can have both simultaneously.**

Here's the breakdown:

## Overlapping Effect: Speed 0
Both Grappled and Restrained set your Speed to 0 and prevent it from increasing. This is the **same effect**, so it doesn't "double" — your Speed is simply 0. Having both conditions doesn't make you "more speedless."

## Distinct Effects That *Do* Stack (Coexist)

| Effect | Grappled | Restrained |
|---|---|---|
| Speed 0 | ✅ | ✅ (redundant) |
| Your attacks vs. others have Disadvantage | ✅ | — |
| Your attacks have Disadvantage | — | ✅ |
| Attacks against you have Advantage | — | ✅ |
| Disadvantage on Dexterity saving throws | — | ✅ |
| Grappler can drag/carry you (extra movement cost) | ✅ | — |

So a creature that is **both Grappled and Restrained** suffers:
- **Speed 0** (from either/both)
- **Disadvantage on all attack rolls** (Disadvantage against targets other than the grappler *and* Disadvantage on all attacks from Restrained — these don't stack further, you just have Disadvantage)
- **Advantage for attackers against you** (from Restrained)
- **Disadvantage on Dexterity saving throws** (from Restrained)
- **Can be dragged/carried by the grappler** (from Grappled)

## Practical Example
This situation arises naturally — for instance, if you use a **Chain** (Equipment) on a creature that already has the Grappled condition and succeed on the DC 13 Strength (Athletics) check, the creature gains the Restrained condition *in addition to* the Grappled condition.

**In summary:** The conditions don't "stack" in the sense of amplifying the same effect, but they apply simultaneously, and their *unique* effects all apply to the creature.

#### Difficult Terrain  
If a space is Difficult Terrain, every foot of movement in that space costs 1 extra foot. For example, moving 5 feet through Difficult Terrain costs 10 feet of movement. Difficult Terrain isn't cumulative; either a space is Difficult Terrain or it isn't.  
A space is Difficult Terrain if the space contains any of the following or something similar:  
- A creature that isn't Tiny or your ally
- Furniture that is sized for creatures of your size or larger
- Heavy snow, ice, rubble, or undergrowth
- Liquid that's between shin- and waist-deep
- A narrow opening sized for a creature one size smaller than you
- A slope of 20 degrees or more

#### Difficult Terrain  
Combatants are often slowed down by Difficult Terrain. Low furniture, rubble, undergrowth, steep stairs, snow, and shallow bogs are examples of Difficult Terrain.  
Every foot of movement in Difficult Terrain costs 1 extra foot, even if multiple things in a space count as Difficult Terrain.

#### Climbing  
While you're climbing, each foot of movement costs 1 extra foot (2 extra feet in Difficult Terrain). You ignore this extra cost if you have a Climb Speed and use it to climb.
At the GM's option, climbing a slippery surface or one with few handholds might require a successful DC 15 Strength (Athletics) check.

#### Swimming  
While you're swimming, each foot of movement costs 1 extra foot (2 extra feet in Difficult Terrain). You ignore this extra cost if you have a Swim Speed and use it to swim. At the GM's option, moving any distance in rough water might require a successful DC 15 Strength (Athletics) check.

#### Crawling  
While you're crawling, each foot of movement costs 1 extra foot (2 extra feet in Difficult Terrain). _See also_ "Speed."

### Special Movement  
If a party can travel at a high Speed for an extended time, as with a spell such as _Wind Walk_ or a magic item such as a _Carpet of Flying_, translate the party's Speed into travel rates using these rules:  
**Miles per hour** = Speed ÷ 10
**Miles per day** (Normal pace) = Miles per hour × number of hours traveled (typically 8)
**Fast pace** = Miles per day × 1⅓ (round down)
**Slow pace** = Miles per day × 2/3 (round down)  
If the characters are flying or their special movement allows them to ignore Difficult Terrain, they can move at a Fast pace regardless of the terrain.

#### Chain (5 GP)  
As a Utilize action, you can wrap a Chain around an unwilling creature within 5 feet of yourself that has the Grappled, Incapacitated, or Restrained condition if you succeed on a DC 13 Strength (Athletics) check. If the creature's legs are bound, the creature has the Restrained condition until it escapes. Escaping the Chain requires the creature to make a successful DC 18 Dexterity (Acrobatics) check as an action. Bursting the Chain requires a successful DC 20 Strength (Athletics) check as an action.

#### Restrained [Condition]  
While you have the Restrained condition, you experience the following effects.  
_Speed 0._ Your Speed is 0 and can't increase.  
_Attacks Affected._ Attack rolls against you have Advantage, and your attack rolls have Disadvantage.  
_Saving Throws Affected._ You have Disadvantage on Dexterity saving throws.

#### Grappling  
A creature can grapple another creature. Characters typically grapple by using an Unarmed Strike. Many monsters have special attacks that allow them to quickly grapple prey. However a grapple is initiated, it follows these rules. _See also_ "Unarmed Strike" and "Grappled."  
_Grappled Condition._ Successfully grappling a creature gives it the Grappled condition.  
_One Grapple per Hand._ A creature must have a hand free to grapple another creature. Some stat blocks and game effects allow a creature to grapple using a tentacle, a maw, or another body part. Whatever part a grappler uses, it can grapple only one creature at a time with that part, and the grappler can't use that part to target another creature unless it ends the grapple.  
_Ending a Grapple._ A Grappled creature can use its action to make a Strength (Athletics) or Dexterity (Acrobatics) check against the grapple's escape DC, ending the condition on itself on a success. The condition also ends if the grappler has the Incapacitated condition or if the distance between the Grappled target and the grappler exceeds the grapple's range. In addition, the grappler can release the target at any time (no action required).

#### Manacles (2 GP)  
As a Utilize action, you can use Manacles to bind an unwilling Small or Medium creature within 5 feet of yourself that has the Grappled, Incapacitated, or Restrained condition if you succeed on a DC 13 Dexterity (Sleight of Hand) check. While bound, a creature has Disadvantage on attack rolls, and the creature is Restrained if the Manacles are attached to a chain or hook that is fixed in place. Escaping the Manacles requires a successful DC 20 Dexterity (Sleight of Hand) check as an action. Bursting them requires a successful DC 25 Strength (Athletics) check as an action.  
Each set of Manacles comes with a key. Without the key, a creature can use Thieves' Tools to pick the Manacles' lock with a successful DC 15 Dexterity (Sleight of Hand) check.

#### Grappler  
_General Feat (Prerequisite: Level 4+, Strength or Dexterity 13+)_  
You gain the following benefits.  
_Ability Score Increase._ Increase your Strength or Dexterity score by 1, to a maximum of 20.  
_Punch and Grab._ When you hit a creature with an Unarmed Strike as part of the Attack action on your turn, you can use both the Damage and the Grapple option. You can use this benefit only once per turn.  
_Attack Advantage._ You have Advantage on attack rolls against a creature Grappled by you.  
_Fast Wrestler._ You don't have to spend extra movement to move a creature Grappled by you if the creature is your size or smaller.

#### Difficult Terrain  
If a space is Difficult Terrain, every foot of movement in that space costs 1 extra foot. For example, moving 5 feet through Difficult Terrain costs 10 feet of movement. Difficult Terrain isn't cumulative; either a space is Difficult Terrain or it isn't.  
A space is Difficult Terrain if the space contains any of the following or something similar:  
- A creature that isn't Tiny or your ally
- Furniture that is sized for creatures of your size or larger
- Heavy snow, ice, rubble, or undergrowth
- Liquid that's between shin- and waist-deep
- A narrow opening sized for a creature one size smaller than you
- A slope of 20 degrees or more

#### Difficult Terrain  
Combatants are often slowed down by Difficult Terrain. Low furniture, rubble, undergrowth, steep stairs, snow, and shallow bogs are examples of Difficult Terrain.  
Every foot of movement in Difficult Terrain costs 1 extra foot, even if multiple things in a space count as Difficult Terrain.

#### Climbing  
While you're climbing, each foot of movement costs 1 extra foot (2 extra feet in Difficult Terrain). You ignore this extra cost if you have a Climb Speed and use it to climb.
At the GM's option, climbing a slippery surface or one with few handholds might require a successful DC 15 Strength (Athletics) check.

#### Swimming  
While you're swimming, each foot of movement costs 1 extra foot (2 extra feet in Difficult Terrain). You ignore this extra cost if you have a Swim Speed and use it to swim. At the GM's option, moving any distance in rough water might require a successful DC 15 Strength (Athletics) check.

#### Crawling  
While you're crawling, each foot of movement costs 1 extra foot (2 extra feet in Difficult Terrain). _See also_ "Speed."

### Special Movement  
If a party can travel at a high Speed for an extended time, as with a spell such as _Wind Walk_ or a magic item such as a _Carpet of Flying_, translate the party's Speed into travel rates using these rules:  
**Miles per hour** = Speed ÷ 10
**Miles per day** (Normal pace) = Miles per hour × number of hours traveled (typically 8)
**Fast pace** = Miles per day × 1⅓ (round down)
**Slow pace** = Miles per day × 2/3 (round down)  
If the characters are flying or their special movement allows them to ignore Difficult Terrain, they can move at a Fast pace regardless of the terrain.

Yes, flying through Difficult Terrain costs extra movement—**unless** the method of flying allows the creature to ignore Difficult Terrain.

According to the SRD 5.2.1, Difficult Terrain normally costs 1 extra foot of movement per foot moved ([1], [2]). The rules for climbing, swimming, and crawling explicitly state that moving through Difficult Terrain while using those modes costs **2 extra feet** per foot moved ([3]–[5]), but **flying is not listed** among those special movement types with modified Difficult Terrain rules.

However, [6] notes that if a creature’s special movement (such as flying via *Wind Walk* or a *Carpet of Flying*) **allows them to ignore Difficult Terrain**, then they do so. This implies that **flying does not automatically ignore Difficult Terrain**—only if the specific flying ability or feature says it does.

Therefore, **a creature flying through Difficult Terrain must pay the standard Difficult Terrain cost (1 extra foot per foot moved) unless its flying ability explicitly lets it ignore Difficult Terrain.**

#### Level 13: Relentless Hunter  
Taking damage can't break your Concentration on _Hunter's Mark_.

#### Hunter's Mark  
_Level 1 Divination (Ranger)_  
**Casting Time:** Bonus Action
**Range:** 90 feet
**Components:** V
**Duration:** Concentration, up to 1 hour  
You magically mark one creature you can see within range as your quarry. Until the spell ends, you deal an extra 1d6 Force damage to the target whenever you hit it with an attack roll. You also have Advantage on any Wisdom (Perception or Survival) check you make to find it.  
If the target drops to 0 Hit Points before this spell ends, you can take a Bonus Action to move the mark to a new creature you can see within range.  
_Using a Higher-Level Spell Slot._ Your Concentration can last longer with a spell slot of level 3–4 (up to 8 hours) or 5+ (up to 24 hours).

#### Concentration  
Some spells and other effects require Concentration to remain active, as specified in their descriptions. If the effect's creator loses Concentration, the effect ends. If the effect has a maximum duration, the effect's description specifies how long the creator can concentrate on it: up to 1 minute, 1 hour, or some other duration. The creator can end Concentration at any time (no action required). The following factors break Concentration.  
_Another Concentration Effect._ You lose Concentration on an effect the moment you start casting a spell that requires Concentration or activate another effect that requires Concentration.  
_Damage._ If you take damage, you must succeed on a Constitution saving throw to maintain Concentration. The DC equals 10 or half the damage taken (round down), whichever number is higher, up to a maximum DC of 30.  
_Incapacitated or Dead._ Your Concentration ends if you have the Incapacitated condition or you die.

You have Advantage on attack rolls against the creature currently marked by your _Hunter's Mark_.

Once per turn when you deal damage to a creature marked by your _Hunter's Mark_, you can also deal that spell's extra damage to a different creature that you can see within 30 feet of the first creature.

#### Level 15: Superior Hunter's Defense  
When you take damage, you can take a Reaction to give yourself Resistance to that damage and any other damage of the same type until the end of the current turn.

#### Difficult Terrain  
If a space is Difficult Terrain, every foot of movement in that space costs 1 extra foot. For example, moving 5 feet through Difficult Terrain costs 10 feet of movement. Difficult Terrain isn't cumulative; either a space is Difficult Terrain or it isn't.  
A space is Difficult Terrain if the space contains any of the following or something similar:  
- A creature that isn't Tiny or your ally
- Furniture that is sized for creatures of your size or larger
- Heavy snow, ice, rubble, or undergrowth
- Liquid that's between shin- and waist-deep
- A narrow opening sized for a creature one size smaller than you
- A slope of 20 degrees or more

#### Difficult Terrain  
Combatants are often slowed down by Difficult Terrain. Low furniture, rubble, undergrowth, steep stairs, snow, and shallow bogs are examples of Difficult Terrain.  
Every foot of movement in Difficult Terrain costs 1 extra foot, even if multiple things in a space count as Difficult Terrain.

#### Climbing  
While you're climbing, each foot of movement costs 1 extra foot (2 extra feet in Difficult Terrain). You ignore this extra cost if you have a Climb Speed and use it to climb.
At the GM's option, climbing a slippery surface or one with few handholds might require a successful DC 15 Strength (Athletics) check.

#### Swimming  
While you're swimming, each foot of movement costs 1 extra foot (2 extra feet in Difficult Terrain). You ignore this extra cost if you have a Swim Speed and use it to swim. At the GM's option, moving any distance in rough water might require a successful DC 15 Strength (Athletics) check.

#### Crawling  
While you're crawling, each foot of movement costs 1 extra foot (2 extra feet in Difficult Terrain). _See also_ "Speed."

### Special Movement  
If a party can travel at a high Speed for an extended time, as with a spell such as _Wind Walk_ or a magic item such as a _Carpet of Flying_, translate the party's Speed into travel rates using these rules:  
**Miles per hour** = Speed ÷ 10
**Miles per day** (Normal pace) = Miles per hour × number of hours traveled (typically 8)
**Fast pace** = Miles per day × 1⅓ (round down)
**Slow pace** = Miles per day × 2/3 (round down)  
If the characters are flying or their special movement allows them to ignore Difficult Terrain, they can move at a Fast pace regardless of the terrain.

#### Truesight  
If you have Truesight, your vision is enhanced within a specified range. Within that range, your vision pierces through the following:

_Level 2 Illusion (Bard, Sorcerer, Warlock, Wizard)_  
**Casting Time:** Action
**Range:** Self
**Components:** V, S
**Duration:** 1 minute  
Three illusory duplicates of yourself appear in your space. Until the spell ends, the duplicates move with you and mimic your actions, shifting position so it's impossible to track which image is real.  
Each time a creature hits you with an attack roll during the spell's duration, roll a d6 for each of your remaining duplicates. If any of the d6s rolls a 3 or higher, one of the duplicates is hit instead of you, and the duplicate is destroyed. The duplicates otherwise ignore all other damage and effects. The spell ends when all three duplicates are destroyed.  
A creature is unaffected by this spell if it has the Blinded condition, Blindsight, or Truesight.

#### Mirror of Life Trapping  
_Wondrous Item, Very Rare_  
When this 4-foot-tall, 2-foot-wide mirror is viewed indirectly, its surface shows faint images of creatures. The mirror weighs 50 pounds, and it has AC 11, HP 10, Immunity to Poison and Psychic damage, and Vulnerability to Bludgeoning damage. It shatters and is destroyed when reduced to 0 Hit Points.  
If the mirror is hanging on a vertical surface and you are within 5 feet of it, you can take a Magic action and use a command word to activate it. It remains activated until you take a Magic action and repeat the command word to deactivate it.  
Any creature other than you that sees its reflection in the activated mirror while within 30 feet of the mirror must succeed on a DC 15 Charisma saving throw or be trapped, along with anything it is wearing or carrying, in one of the mirror's twelve extradimensional cells. A creature that knows the mirror's nature makes the save with Advantage, and Constructs succeed on the save automatically.  
An extradimensional cell is an infinite expanse filled with thick fog that reduces visibility to 10 feet. Creatures trapped in the mirror's cells don't age, and they don't need to eat, drink, or sleep. A creature trapped within a cell can escape using magic that permits planar travel. Otherwise, the creature is confined to the cell until freed.  
If the mirror traps a creature but its twelve extradimensional cells are already occupied, the mirror frees one trapped creature at random to accommodate the new prisoner. A freed creature appears in an unoccupied space within sight of the mirror but facing away from it. If the mirror is shattered, all creatures it contains are freed and appear in unoccupied spaces near it.  
While within 5 feet of the mirror, you can take a Magic action to name one creature trapped in it or call out a particular cell by number. The creature named or contained in the named cell appears as an image on the mirror's surface. You and the creature can then communicate.

You gain the following benefits.

A handheld steel Mirror is useful for personal cosmetics but also for peeking around corners and reflecting light as a signal.

_Wondrous Item, Legendary (Requires Attunement)_

**Answer:** No, the Bless spell does not break when a target becomes Charmed.

**Reasoning:**  
- **Bless (SRD 5.2.1, spells.md)** requires the caster to maintain **concentration** for up to 1 minute, allowing the target to add 1d4 to attack rolls or saving throws while the spell is active.  
- **Charmed (SRD 5.2.1, rules‑glossary.md)** imposes conditions such as “Can't Harm the Charmer” and “Social Advantage,” but it does **not** list breaking concentration or affecting spell effects as part of its definition.  
- The Charmed condition only restricts the charmed creature’s ability to target or harm the charmer and grants the charmer advantage on social checks. It does **not** interfere with the mechanics of Bless, which merely adds a bonus to rolls.  
- Since Bless’s duration and concentration are independent of the target’s condition, a target that becomes Charmed while under Bless continues to benefit from the spell’s effects until the spell’s duration ends or the caster loses concentration.

Therefore, a Cleric concentrating on Bless can keep the spell active even if one of its targets is later Charmed.

**Answer:** Yes, a Tiny familiar can share space with the wizard and provide half cover.

**Reasoning:**

No, a Tiny familiar cannot share space with its wizard or provide Half Cover.

According to the SRD 5.2.1 rules on movement and positioning (not fully quoted in your context but part of the core rules), **creatures cannot willingly end their movement in another creature’s space**, regardless of size—unless a specific rule says otherwise (such as the Halfling’s *Halfling Nimbleness*, which explicitly allows moving through but **not stopping** in a larger creature’s space).

Since the *Find Familiar* spell does not grant an exception allowing the familiar to occupy the same space as the wizard, the familiar must remain in its own space. Therefore, it cannot share the wizard’s space.

Because it cannot occupy the same space, it also cannot provide **Half Cover** to the wizard simply by being adjacent or nearby. Cover is determined by obstacles or creatures **between** the attacker and the target. A Tiny creature does not block enough of a Medium creature’s body to grant cover unless it is **between** the attacker and the wizard—and even then, a Tiny creature typically does **not** provide cover to a Medium creature due to its small size (per general cover rules in the SRD).

Thus, under SRD 5.2.1 rules:  
- A Tiny familiar **cannot share space** with the wizard.  
- A Tiny familiar **does not provide Half Cover** to the wizard.

# Tiny Familiar Sharing Space & Providing Half Cover

## Sharing Space

**Yes, a Tiny familiar can share a space with the Wizard.**

The SRD 5.2.1 does not contain a general rule that prevents creatures of different sizes from occupying the same space. The only size-based space rule provided is **Halfling Nimbleness** (from the Halfling origin), which states:

> *"You can move through the space of any creature that is a size larger than you, but you can't stop in the same space."*

This trait is specific to Halflings and explicitly says a Small creature **cannot stop** in the same space as a larger creature. However, a Tiny familiar is **one size smaller** than a Small Halfling. The Halfling Nimbleness rule only addresses moving through spaces of creatures **one size larger** — it doesn't address Tiny creatures at all.

Since the SRD 5.2.1 provides **no general rule** prohibiting a Tiny creature from sharing a space with a Medium (or larger) creature, and the only relevant size-based movement restriction (Halfling Nimbleness) doesn't apply to Tiny creatures, a Tiny familiar **can share the Wizard's space**.

## Providing Half Cover

3. Roll the attack; if Advantage is granted, roll twice and use the higher result, then compare it to the target’s AC (including the +5 cover bonus).

Thus, the net result is **Advantage on the attack roll against a target with +5 AC from Three‑Quarters Cover**. The Advantage can increase the likelihood of hitting despite the higher AC, but the +5 AC still must be overcome.

To determine if Thunderwave on the Roper can end its grapple by pushing the Roper away, we need to understand the Grappled condition and how it interacts with being moved by an effect like Thunderwave.

The Grappled condition states that the grappler can drag or carry the grappled creature when it moves, but it doesn't explicitly state that the grappled creature can't move the grappler. However, the key point is that the Grappled condition is tied to the grappler, not the grappled creature's position relative to the grappler.

When the Roper casts Thunderwave, it pushes creatures away from it. If the Roper is grappling a creature, this means the Roper is being pushed away from the grappled creature. The question then is whether this movement ends the grapple.

The rules for the Grappled condition don't specify that the grapple ends if the grappler is moved away from the grappled creature. Instead, they focus on the grappler's ability to move the grappled creature. 

Since there's no explicit rule stating that a grapple ends when the grappler is moved away from the grappled creature, and given that the Roper's tentacle is what's grappling (not its body position), the grapple should remain as long as the tentacle remains attached and hasn't been damaged or otherwise affected.

Therefore, Thunderwave on the Roper does not end its grapple by pushing the Roper away, as the condition is dependent on the tentacle's grip, not the Roper's position relative to the grappled creature.

# Thunderwave and the Roper's Grapple

**No, Thunderwave cannot end the Roper's grapple by pushing the Roper away.**

Here's why:

1. **Thunderwave pushes creatures away from the caster.** The spell's effect moves creatures in relation to the caster's position.

2. **The Grappled condition's "Movable" rule** states that the grappler (the Roper) can drag or carry the grappled creature when *it* moves. This means if the grappled creature is pushed, the Roper can simply drag the grappled creature along with it — the grapple itself is not broken by forced movement of the grappled creature.

3. **The grapple ends only under specific conditions:** The grappled creature escapes (via the escape DC 14 check), the grappler becomes Incapacitated, or the grappler voluntarily releases the grapple. Forced movement of the grappled creature does not end the grapple.

4. **The tentacle itself** is what maintains the grapple. Even if the Roper's body were somehow pushed, the tentacle (AC 20, HP 10) would need to be destroyed to free the grappled creature. The tentacle is a separate entity with its own hit points and AC.

So Thunderwave would deal damage to the Roper, but it would not break the grapple. The grappled creature would still have Speed 0 and remain grappled.

Temporary Hit Points can't be added together. If you have Temporary Hit Points and receive more of them, you decide whether to keep the ones you have or to gain the new ones. For example, if a spell grants you 12 Temporary Hit Points when you already have 10, you can have 12 or 10, not 22.

Some spells and other effects confer Temporary Hit Points, which are a buffer against losing actual Hit Points, as explained below.

The healing spells you cast on others heal you as well. Immediately after you cast a spell with a spell slot that restores Hit Points to one or more creatures other than yourself, you regain Hit Points equal to 2 plus the spell slot's level.

#### They Don't Stack  
Temporary Hit Points can't be added together. If you have Temporary Hit Points and receive more of them, you decide whether to keep the ones you have or to gain the new ones. For example, if a spell grants you 12 Temporary Hit Points when you already have 10, you can have 12 or 10, not 22.

#### Level 3: Dark One's Blessing  
When you reduce an enemy to 0 Hit Points, you gain Temporary Hit Points equal to your Charisma modifier plus your Warlock level (minimum of 1 Temporary Hit Point). You also gain this benefit if someone else reduces an enemy within 10 feet of you to 0 Hit Points.

### Temporary Hit Points  
Some spells and other effects confer Temporary Hit Points, which are a buffer against losing actual Hit Points, as explained below.

#### Temporary Hit Points  
Temporary Hit Points are granted by certain effects and act as a buffer against losing real Hit Points. _See also_ "Playing the Game" ("Damage and Healing").

#### Level 6: Blessed Healer  
The healing spells you cast on others heal you as well. Immediately after you cast a spell with a spell slot that restores Hit Points to one or more creatures other than yourself, you regain Hit Points equal to 2 plus the spell slot's level.

retrieved_context.text:
#### They're Not Hit Points or Healing  
Temporary Hit Points can't be added to your Hit Points, healing can't restore them, and receiving Temporary Hit Points doesn't count as healing. Because Temporary Hit Points aren't Hit Points, a creature can be at full Hit Points and receive Temporary Hit Points.  
If you have 0 Hit Points, receiving Temporary Hit Points doesn't restore you to consciousness. Only true healing can save you.

Nothing can pass into or out of the Emanation. A creature or object inside the Emanation can't be damaged by attacks or effects originating from outside, nor can a creature inside the Emanation damage anything outside it. Once this property is used, it can't be used again until the next dawn.

A Bonus Action is a special action that you can take on the same turn that you take an action. You can't take more than one Bonus Action on a turn, and you have a Bonus Action to take only if a rule explicitly says so. _See also_ "Playing the Game" ("Actions").

Various class features, spells, and other abilities let you take an additional action on your turn called a Bonus Action. # No, They Cannot Stack — You Can't Use Both at the Same Time

A Barbarian's **Rage** grants **Resistance** to Bludgeoning, Piercing, and Slashing damage. The **Heavy Armor Master** feat reduces Bludgeoning, Piercing, and Slashing damage taken from nonmagical attacks by 3.

However, **Rage cannot be used while wearing Heavy armor.** From the Rage feature:

> *"You can enter it as a Bonus Action **if you aren't wearing Heavy armor.**"*

And:

> *"The Rage lasts until the end of your next turn, and it ends early if you don Heavy armor..."*

Since **Heavy Armor Master** requires you to be wearing Heavy armor to apply its damage reduction, and **Rage explicitly cannot be active while wearing Heavy armor**, the two features are **mutually exclusive**. You cannot benefit from both simultaneously.

You must choose one or the other — either Rage (with Resistance) or Heavy armor (with Heavy Armor Master's flat damage reduction) — but never both at once.

#### Help [Action]  
When you take the Help action, you do one of the following.  
_Assist an Ability Check._ Choose one of your skill or tool proficiencies and one ally who is near
enough for you to assist verbally or physically when they make an ability check. That ally has Advantage on the next ability check they make with the chosen skill or tool. This benefit expires if the ally doesn't use it before the start of your next turn. The GM has final say on whether your assistance is possible.  
_Assist an Attack Roll._ You momentarily distract an enemy within 5 feet of you, giving Advantage to the next attack roll by one of your allies against that enemy. This benefit expires at the start of your next turn.

#### Initiative  
Initiative determines the order of turns during combat. The combat rules in "Playing the Game" explain how to roll Initiative.  
Sometimes a GM might have combatants use their Initiative scores instead of rolling Initiative. Your Initiative score equals 10 plus your Dexterity modifier. If you have Advantage on Initiative rolls, increase your Initiative score by 5. If you have Disadvantage on those rolls, decrease that score by 5. _See also_ "Playing the Game" ("Combat").

### Origin Feats  
#### Alert  
_Origin Feat_  
You gain the following benefits.  
_Initiative Proficiency._ When you roll Initiative, you can add your Proficiency Bonus to the roll.  
_Initiative Swap._ Immediately after you roll Initiative, you can swap your Initiative with the Initiative of one willing ally in the same combat. You can't make this swap if you or the ally has the Incapacitated condition.

#### Interactions with Rerolls  
When you have Advantage or Disadvantage and something in the game lets you reroll or replace the d20, you can reroll or replace only one die, not both. You choose which one.  
For example, if you have Heroic Inspiration (see the sidebar below) and roll a 3 and an 18 on an ability check that has Advantage or Disadvantage, you could expend your Heroic Inspiration to reroll one of those dice, not both of them.  
> **Heroic Inspiration**
>
> Sometimes the GM or a rule gives you Heroic Inspiration. If you have Heroic Inspiration, you can expend it to reroll any die immediately after rolling it, and you must use the new roll.
>
> _Only One at a Time._ You can never have more than one instance of Heroic Inspiration. If something gives you Heroic Inspiration and you already have it, you can give it to a player character in your group who lacks it.
>
> _Gaining Heroic Inspiration._ Your GM can give you Heroic Inspiration for a variety of reasons. Typically, GMs award it when you do something particularly heroic, in character, or entertaining. It's a reward for making the game more fun for everyone playing.
>
> Other rules might allow your character to gain Heroic Inspiration independent of the GM's decision. For example, Human characters start each day with Heroic Inspiration.

#### Level 18: Superior Inspiration  
When you roll Initiative, you regain expended uses of Bardic Inspiration until you have two if you have fewer than that.

#### Initiative  
Initiative determines the order of turns during combat. When combat starts, every participant rolls Initiative; they make a Dexterity check that determines their place in the Initiative order. The GM rolls for monsters. For a group of identical creatures, the GM makes a single roll, so each member of the group has the same Initiative.  
**Surprise.** If a combatant is surprised by combat starting, that combatant has Disadvantage on their Initiative roll. For example, if an ambusher starts combat while hidden from a foe who is unaware that combat is starting, that foe is surprised.  
**Initiative Order.** A combatant's check total is called their Initiative count, or Initiative for short. The GM ranks the combatants, from highest to lowest Initiative. This is the order in which they act during each round. The Initiative order remains the same from round to round.  
**Ties.** If a tie occurs, the GM decides the order among tied monsters, and the players decide the order among tied characters. The GM decides the order if the tie is between a monster and a player character.

When a Wizard **Readies** the *Fireball* spell, the spell slot is **expended when the spell is initially cast**, not when the trigger occurs.

Readying a spell involves casting it as normal (using an action and expending the spell slot) but holding its energy until a specified trigger occurs. This is clarified in the general rules for the Ready action and spellcasting (though not fully detailed in the provided SRD excerpts). However, based on standard SRD 5.2.1 rules:

- Casting a spell with a casting time of **1 action** as a **Ready action** still requires you to **cast the spell** on your turn.
- That means you **expend the spell slot** and provide all components when you Ready it.
- If the trigger never occurs, the spell is lost, but the slot is still spent.

Thus, for *Fireball*, the **spell slot is expended at the time of Ready**, not at the trigger.
