## Components  
A spell's components are physical requirements the spellcaster must meet to cast the spell. Each spell's description indicates whether it requires Verbal (V), Somatic (S), or Material (M) components. If the spellcaster can't provide one or more of a spell's components, the spellcaster can't cast the spell.

### Verbal (V)  
A Verbal component is the chanting of esoteric words that sound like nonsense to the uninitiated. The words must be uttered in a normal speaking voice. The words themselves aren't the source of the spell's power; rather, the particular combination of sounds, with specific pitch and resonance, sets the threads of magic in motion. Thus, a creature who is gagged or in an area of magical silence can't cast a spell with a Verbal component.

### Material (M)  
A Material component is a particular material used in a spell's casting, as specified in parentheses in the Components entry. These materials aren't consumed by the spell unless the spell's description states otherwise. The spellcaster must have a hand free to access them, but it can be the same hand used to perform Somatic components, if any.  
If a spell doesn't consume its materials and doesn't specify a cost for them, a spellcaster can use a Component Pouch (see "Equipment") instead of providing the materials specified in the spell, or the
spellcaster can substitute a Spellcasting Focus if the caster has a feature that allows that substitution. To use a Component Pouch, you must have a hand free to reach into it, and to use a Spellcasting Focus, you must hold it unless its description says otherwise (see "Equipment" for descriptions).

### Somatic (S)  
A Somatic component is a forceful gesticulation or an intricate set of gestures. A spellcaster must use at least one of their hands to perform these movements.

#### Spellcasting  
If a monster can cast any spells, its stat block lists the spells and provides the monster's spellcasting ability, spell save DC (if any spells require a saving throw), and spell attack bonus (if any spells require an attack roll). Unless noted otherwise, a spell of level 1 or higher is always cast at its lowest possible level and can't be cast at a higher level.  
A monster's spell can have special rules or restrictions. For example, a green hag can cast the _Invisibility_ spell, but the spell has a "self only" restriction, which means the spell affects only the hag.  
_Spell Components._ The Spellcasting trait notes whether the monster's spellcasting ignores the need for certain spell components. If any spell components are required, describe the monster's use of Verbal, Somatic, or Material components to signal to characters that it is casting a spell. A monster that requires Material components has them.  
_Casting Times of 1+ Minutes._ If a spell has a casting time of 1 minute or more yet is listed in a spellcasting action, the monster doesn't cast the spell in just one action unless the action's description states otherwise; the monster must take the Magic action on each of its turns and maintain Concentration to cast the spell, as described in "Rules Glossary."

**Wall of Force**  
- **Physical properties:** 1/4‑inch thick, invisible, no material composition.  
- **HP / AC:** Immune to all damage; cannot be hit, thus no HP or AC.  
- **Effect on a creature whose space it occupies:** The creature is pushed to one side of the wall (caster chooses).  
- **How it can be destroyed:** Only a **Disintegrate** spell destroys it instantly; it is immune to all other damage, dispelling, and physical attacks.

**Wall of Ice**  
- **Physical properties:** 1‑foot thick.  
- **HP / AC:** Each 10‑foot panel has **AC 12** and **30 HP** per 10‑foot section (so a 10‑ft panel = 30 HP).  
- **Effect on a creature whose space it occupies:** The creature is pushed to one side; on a failed Dexterity save it takes **10d6 Cold damage** (half on a success).  
- **How it can be destroyed:** Damage reduces HP; **Fire** deals double damage (vulnerability). When a panel’s HP reach 0, it is destroyed and leaves a sheet of frigid air that deals **5d6 Cold damage** to any creature moving through it for the first time each turn.

**Wall of Stone**  
- **Physical properties:** 6‑inch thick (standard) or 3‑inch thick (alternative).  
- **HP / AC:** Each 10‑ft × 10‑ft panel has **AC 15** and **30 HP per inch of thickness**.  
  - 6‑inch wall: 30 HP × 6 = 180 HP per panel.  
  - 3‑inch wall: 30 HP × 3 = 90 HP per panel.  
- **Effect on a creature whose space it occupies:** The creature is pushed to one side. If the wall would fully enclose the creature, it may make a Dexterity saving throw; on a success it can use its Reaction to move up to its Speed to avoid being enclosed.  
- **How it can be destroyed:** Damage reduces HP; the wall is immune to Poison and Psychic damage. Reducing a panel to 0 HP destroys it, and connected panels may collapse at the GM’s discretion. The wall persists for the spell’s duration unless concentration is broken; maintaining concentration makes it permanent.

**Summary Comparison**

| Feature | Wall of Force | Wall of Ice | Wall of Stone |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Thickness** | 1/4 in (effectively non‑physical) | 1 ft | 6 in (or 3 in) |
| **HP / AC** | No HP, immune to damage; no AC | AC 12, 30 HP per 10‑ft panel | AC 15, 30 HP per inch (180 HP for 6‑in, 90 HP for 3‑in) |
| **Push effect** | Pushes creature to chosen side | Pushes creature; Dexterity save vs 10d6 Cold | Pushes creature; optional Dexterity save to avoid enclosure |
| **Damage on appearance** | None (only push) | 10d6 Cold on failed save | None (only push) |
| **Vulnerabilities / Immunities** | Immune to all damage; destroyed only by Disintegrate | Vulnerable to Fire, immune to Cold, Poison, Psychic | Immune to Poison & Psychic; vulnerable to nothing special |
| **Method of destruction** | Disintegrate only | Fire damage (×2) reduces HP; frigid‑air damage after destruction | Physical damage reduces HP; collapses if connected panels lose HP |
| **Additional effects** | Blocks ethereal travel | Frigid‑air damage after destruction | Can be shaped to bridge gaps, become permanent with sustained concentration |

These differences highlight that **Wall of Force** is purely magical and immune to conventional damage, **Wall of Ice** is fragile but deals cold damage and is vulnerable to fire, and **Wall of Stone** is the most durable, requiring physical force (or magical damage) to breach, with optional shape‑shifting capabilities.

You create a wall of ice on a solid surface within range. You can form it into a hemispherical dome or a globe with a radius of up to 10 feet, or you can shape a flat surface made up of ten 10-foot-square panels. Each panel must be contiguous with another panel. In any form, the wall is 1 foot thick and lasts for the duration.  
If the wall cuts through a creature's space when it appears, the creature is pushed to one side of the wall (you choose which side) and makes a Dexterity saving throw, taking 10d6 Cold damage on a failed save or half as much damage on a successful one.  
The wall is an object that can be damaged and thus breached. It has AC 12 and 30 Hit Points per 10-foot section, and it has Immunity to Cold, Poison, and Psychic damage and Vulnerability to Fire damage. Reducing a 10-foot section of wall to 0 Hit Points destroys it and leaves behind a sheet of frigid air in the space the wall occupied.  
A creature moving through the sheet of frigid air for the first time on a turn makes a Constitution saving throw, taking 5d6 Cold damage on a failed save or half as much damage on a successful one.
_Using a Higher-Level Spell Slot._ The damage the wall deals when it appears increases by 2d6 and the damage from passing through the sheet of frigid air increases by 1d6 for each spell slot level above 6.

#### Wall of Stone  
_Level 5 Evocation (Druid, Sorcerer, Wizard)_  
**Casting Time:** Action
**Range:** 120 feet
**Components:** V, S, M (a cube of granite)
**Duration:** Concentration, up to 10 minutes  
A nonmagical wall of solid stone springs into existence at a point you choose within range. The wall is 6 inches thick and is composed of ten 10-foot-by-10-foot panels. Each panel must be contiguous with another panel. Alternatively, you can create 10-foot-by-20-foot panels that are only 3 inches thick.  
If the wall cuts through a creature's space when it appears, the creature is pushed to one side of the wall (you choose which side). If a creature would be surrounded on all sides by the wall (or the wall and another solid surface), that creature can make a Dexterity saving throw. On a success, it can use its Reaction to move up to its Speed so that it is no longer enclosed by the wall.  
The wall can have any shape you desire, though it can't occupy the same space as a creature or object. The wall doesn't need to be vertical or rest on a firm foundation. It must, however, merge with and be solidly supported by existing stone. Thus, you can use this spell to bridge a chasm or create a ramp.  
If you create a span greater than 20 feet in length, you must halve the size of each panel to create supports. You can crudely shape the wall to create battlements and the like.  
The wall is an object made of stone that can be damaged and thus breached. Each panel has AC 15 and 30 Hit Points per inch of thickness, and it has Immunity to Poison and Psychic damage. Reducing a panel to 0 Hit Points destroys it and might cause connected panels to collapse at the GM's discretion.  
If you maintain your Concentration on this spell for its full duration, the wall becomes permanent and can't be dispelled. Otherwise, the wall disappears when the spell ends.

**Range:** 120 feet
**Components:** V, S, M (a shard of glass)

An Invisible wall of force springs into existence at a point you choose within range. The wall appears in any orientation you choose, as a horizontal or vertical barrier or at an angle. You can form it into a hemispherical dome or a globe with a radius of up to 10 feet, or you can shape a flat surface made up of ten 10-foot-by-10-foot panels. Each panel must be contiguous with another panel. In any form, the wall is 1/4 inch thick and lasts for the duration. If the wall cuts through a creature's space when it appears, the creature is pushed to one side of the wall (you choose which side).  
Nothing can physically pass through the wall. It is immune to all damage and can't be dispelled by _Dispel Magic_. A _Disintegrate_ spell destroys the wall instantly, however. The wall also extends into the Ethereal Plane and blocks ethereal travel through the wall.

Alternatively, you shape the wall into a globe up to 30 feet in diameter centered on a point within range. The wall lasts for the duration. If you position the wall in a space occupied by a creature, the spell ends instantly without effect. The wall sheds Bright Light within 100 feet and Dim Light for an additional 100 feet. **Wall of Stone**  
- **Physical properties:** 6‑inch thick (standard) or 3‑inch thick (alternative).  
- **HP / AC:** Each 10‑ft × 10‑ft panel has **AC 15** and **30 HP per inch of thickness**.

- **Healing amount:** 5d8 + spellcasting ability modifier per target (up to six targets). The healing increases by 1d8 for each spell slot level above 5th.

- **Casting time:** Bonus Action

- **Casting time:** Action

### Physical Properties (HP, AC, Thickness)
* **Wall of Ice:** 1 foot thick. AC 12. 30 Hit Points per 10-foot section.
* **Wall of Stone:** 6 inches thick (for 10-foot-by-10-foot panels) or 3 inches thick (for 10-foot-by-20-foot panels). AC 15. 30 Hit Points per inch of thickness per panel.
* **Wall of Force:** 1/4 inch thick. It is immune to all damage and has no listed AC or HP.

### Effect on a Creature Whose Space They Appear In
* **Wall of Ice:** The creature is pushed to one side of the wall (caster's choice) and must make a Dexterity saving throw. It takes 10d6 Cold damage on a failed save, or half as much on a successful one.
* **Wall of Stone:** The creature is pushed to one side of the wall (caster's choice). If the push would leave the creature surrounded on all sides by the wall (or the wall and another solid surface), the creature can make a Dexterity saving throw. On a success, it can use its Reaction to move up to its Speed so it is no longer enclosed.
* **Wall of Force:** The creature is simply pushed to one side of the wall (caster's choice). 

### How Each Wall Can Be Destroyed
* **Wall of Ice:** Can be breached by dealing enough damage to reduce a 10-foot section to 0 Hit Points. It has Immunity to Cold, Poison, and Psychic damage, and Vulnerability to Fire damage. Destroying a section leaves behind a sheet of frigid air that deals Cold damage to creatures passing through it.
* **Wall of Stone:** Can be breached by dealing enough damage to reduce a panel to 0 Hit Points. It has Immunity to Poison and Psychic damage. Destroying a panel might cause connected panels to collapse at the GM's discretion. If the caster maintains Concentration for the spell's full duration, the wall becomes permanent and can't be dispelled; otherwise, it disappears when the spell ends.
* **Wall of Force:** Because it is immune to all damage, it cannot be destroyed by physical attacks or damaging spells. It also cannot be dispelled by *Dispel Magic*. It can only be destroyed instantly by a *Disintegrate* spell.

_Magical Contagion_  
Fouled potions and alchemical waste can give rise to Sewer Plague, which incubates in sewers and refuse heaps and is sometimes transmitted by creatures that dwell in such areas, including otyughs and rats. Any Humanoid that is wounded by a creature that carries the contagion or that comes into contact with contaminated filth or offal must succeed on a DC 11 Constitution saving throw or become infected with Sewer Plague. A creature suffers the following effects 1d4 days after infection:  
**Fatigue.** The creature gains 1 Exhaustion level.  
**Weakness.** While the creature has any Exhaustion levels, it regains only half the normal number of Hit Points from spending Hit Point Dice.  
**Restlessness.** While the creature has any Exhaustion levels, finishing a Long Rest neither restores lost Hit Points nor reduces the creature's Exhaustion level.  
_Fighting the Contagion._ Daily at dawn, an infected creature makes a DC 11 Constitution saving throw. On a failed save, the creature gains 1 Exhaustion level as its fatigue worsens. The Swallow abilities of the Purple Worm, Remorhaz, and Tarrasque are compared below.

### Number of Creatures Swallowed

* Purple Worm: up to 3 creatures
* Remorhaz: up to 2 creatures
* Tarrasque: up to 6 creatures

* Purple Worm: 17 (5d6) Acid damage, Blinded, and Restrained
* Remorhaz: 10 (3d6) Acid damage + 10 (3d6) Fire damage, Blinded, and Restrained
* Tarrasque: 56 (16d6) Acid damage, Blinded, and Restrained

### Circumstances for Regurgitation

* Purple Worm: regurgitates if it takes 30 damage or more on a single turn from a creature inside it and fails a DC 21 Constitution saving throw
* Remorhaz: regurgitates if it takes 30 damage or more on a single turn from a creature inside it and fails a DC 15 Constitution saving throw
* Tarrasque: regurgitates if it takes 60 damage or more on a single turn from a creature inside it and fails a DC 20 Constitution saving throw

### Additional Notes

* All three creatures have similar behavior when they die: the swallowed creature is no longer Restrained and can escape from the corpse using a certain amount of movement (20 feet for Purple Worm and Tarrasque, 15 feet for Remorhaz), exiting Prone.
* The distance within which the regurgitated creature falls also varies: 5 feet for Purple Worm and Remorhaz, 10 feet for Tarrasque.

## Number of Creatures Swallowed

| Monster | Max Swallowed | Save Type | Save DC |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Purple Worm** | 3 | Strength | 19 |
| **Remorhaz** | 2 | Strength | 19 |
| **Tarrasque** | 6 | Strength | 27 |

All three require the target to be **Grappled** and **Large or smaller**. The Tarrasque can hold the most creatures by far, and its save DC is significantly higher.

| Monster | Damage per Turn | Conditions |
|---|---|---|
| **Purple Worm** | 17 (5d6) Acid | Blinded, Restrained, Total Cover |
| **Remorhaz** | 10 (3d6) Acid + 10 (3d6) Fire | Blinded, Restrained, Total Cover |
| **Tarrasque** | 56 (16d6) Acid | Blinded, Restrained, Total Cover |

| Monster | Damage Threshold | Con Save DC | Escape on Death |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Purple Worm** | 30+ in one turn | DC 21 | 20 ft. movement, exit Prone |
| **Remorhaz** | 30+ in one turn | DC 15 | 15 ft. movement, exit Prone |
| **Tarrasque** | 60+ in one turn | DC 20 | 20 ft. movement, exit Prone |

A swallowed creature (or all swallowed creatures) is regurgitated if the monster takes sufficient internal damage and fails a Constitution saving throw.

  - Trigger: **30+ damage** in one turn from inside.  
  - Save: **DC 21 Constitution**.

  - Trigger: **30+ damage** in one turn from inside.  
  - Save: **DC 15 Constitution**.  
  - On failure: **All** swallowed creatures regurgitated within **5 ft**, **Prone**.

---

- **Tarrasque**: Swallowed creatures are no longer Restrained; escape requires **20 ft** of movement, exit **Prone**.
- **Purple Worm**: Same as Tarrasque—**20 ft** movement, exit **Prone**.
- **Remorhaz**: Escape requires **15 ft** of movement, exit **Prone**.

---

| Feature | Tarrasque | Purple Worm | Remorhaz |
|--------|----------|-------------|----------|
| Max swallowed | 6 | 3 | 2 |
| Damage per turn | 56 Acid | 17 Acid | 10 Acid + 10 Fire |

**Defensive capabilities of Draconic Sorcery vs. Fiend Patron Warlock**

**Draconic Sorcery (Sorcerer subclass)**
- **Draconic Resilience (Level 3)**  
  - **Hit‑point boost:** +3 HP at 3rd level, +1 HP each subsequent Sorcerer level.  
  - **Armor Class:** While not wearing armor, AC = 10 + Dexterity + Charisma. This provides a modest, ability‑score‑dependent AC that scales with Sorcerer levels.  
- **Draconic Spells (starting at 3rd level)**  
  - Spells such as *Alter Self*, *Command*, *Dragon’s Breath*, *Fear*, *Fly*, *Charm Monster*, *Legend Lore*, and *Summon Dragon* include defensive options (e.g., *Alter Self* for resistance, *Fear* for saving throws, *Fly* for mobility, *Charm Monster* to control foes, *Legend Lore* for information, *Summon Dragon* for a powerful ally).  
- **No explicit damage‑reduction or saving‑throw bonuses** beyond the AC boost and spell effects.

**Fiend Patron Warlock**
- **Pact of the Chain (common choice)**  
  - **Fey‑Ancestral Resilience:** +1 AC (or +2 if you have a high Dexterity/Charisma).  
  - **Quasi‑realistic familiar** that can share damage, providing indirect survivability.  
- **Eldritch Invocations (selected at 3rd, 5th, 7th, 9th, 11th, 13th, 15th levels)**  
  - **Dreadful Aspect (3rd):** Enemies have disadvantage on saving throws against your eldritch blast.  
  - **Fey Wanderer (5th):** Advantage on saving throws against being charmed.  
  - **Pact of the Blade (alternative):** +1 AC when wielding the pact weapon.  
  - **Shadow Touched (7th):** Advantage on saving throws against being frightened.  
  - **Pact of the Tome (9th):** Ability to cast higher‑level spells, indirectly improving survivability via stronger defensive spells.  
  - **Pact of the Chain (if chosen):** Familiar can take damage for you, offering a concrete damage‑absorption mechanic.  
- **Warlock Spell List**  
  - Defensive spells include *Shield* (via Mystic Arcanum at 11th level), *Protection* (available at higher levels), *Counterspell*, *Lesser Restoration*, *Banishment*, and *Hold Monster*. These provide active, situational protection and can be prepared or invoked as needed.  

**Comparison**

### Number of Creatures Swallowed
* **Tarrasque:** Up to 6 creatures at a time.
* **Purple Worm:** Up to 3 creatures at a time.
* **Remorhaz:** Up to 2 creatures at a time.

### Damage and Conditions Inflicted
* **Conditions:** For all three monsters, a swallowed creature has the **Blinded** and **Restrained** conditions and has **Total Cover** against attacks and other effects from outside the monster. The **Tarrasque** additionally specifies that the swallowed creature **can't teleport**.
* **Damage (taken at the start of the monster's turn):**
  * **Tarrasque:** 56 (16d6) Acid damage.
  * **Purple Worm:** 17 (5d6) Acid damage.
  * **Remorhaz:** 10 (3d6) Acid damage plus 10 (3d6) Fire damage.

### Circumstances for Regurgitation
* **Damage Threshold & Saving Throw:** If the monster takes a specific amount of damage on a single turn from a creature inside it, it must make a Constitution saving throw at the end of that turn. On a failure, it regurgitates *all* swallowed creatures, who fall with the Prone condition.
  * **Tarrasque:** Taking **60 or more damage** triggers a **DC 20** Constitution save. Regurgitated creatures fall within **10 feet** of the tarrasque.
  * **Purple Worm:** Taking **30 or more damage** triggers a **DC 21** Constitution save. Regurgitated creatures fall within **5 feet** of the worm.
  * **Remorhaz:** Taking **30 or more damage** triggers a **DC 15** Constitution save. Regurgitated creatures fall within **5 feet** of the remorhaz.
* **If the Monster Dies:** Swallowed creatures lose the Restrained condition and can escape the corpse, exiting Prone.
  * **Tarrasque & Purple Worm:** Escaping requires **20 feet** of movement.
  * **Remorhaz:** Escaping requires **15 feet** of movement.

The three types of modifiers that can be added to a D20 Test are:

1. **Relevant Ability Modifier** – Added based on the ability score that governs the test (e.g., Strength for Athletics, Dexterity for Acrobatics, Intelligence for Arcana, etc.).
2. **Proficiency Bonus** – Added when the creature has proficiency with the skill, saving throw, weapon, tool, or spell that the test involves.
3. **Circumstantial Bonuses and Penalties** – Added or subtracted by class features, spells, or other game effects that influence the outcome of the test.

**When the Proficiency Bonus is applied to each kind of D20 Test:**

- **Ability Checks:** The Proficiency Bonus is added when the ability check involves a skill or tool with which the creature is proficient. For example, a Strength (Athletics) check made by a proficient character receives the Proficiency Bonus.
- **Saving Throws:** The Proficiency Bonus is added to a saving throw when the creature is proficient in the relevant saving throw (e.g., Dexterity saving throw against a spell that the creature has proficiency in).
- **Attack Rolls:** The Proficiency Bonus is added to an attack roll when the creature is proficient with the weapon, ammunition, or spell used to make the attack. For instance, a proficient fighter using a longsword adds their Proficiency Bonus to the attack roll. 

In each case, the Proficiency Bonus is applied only if the creature has the appropriate proficiency for the specific test being made.

All creatures have a Proficiency Bonus, which reflects the impact that training has on the creature's capabilities. A character's Proficiency Bonus increases as the character gains levels (described in "Character Creation"). A monster's Proficiency Bonus is based on its Challenge Rating (see "Rules Glossary"). The Proficiency Bonus table shows how the bonus is determined. This bonus is applied to a D20 Test when the creature has proficiency in a skill, in a saving throw, or with an item that the creature uses to make the D20 Test. ## D20 Tests  
When the outcome of an action is uncertain, the game uses a d20 roll to determine success or failure. These rolls are called D20 Tests, and they come in three kinds: ability checks, saving throws, and attack rolls. They follow these steps:  
**4: Roll 1d20.** You always want to roll high. If the roll has Advantage or Disadvantage (described later in "Playing the Game"), you roll two d20s, but you use the number from only one of them—the higher one if you have Advantage or the lower one if you have Disadvantage.  
**5: Add Modifiers.** Add these modifiers to the number rolled on the d20:  
- **The Relevant Ability Modifier.** "Playing the Game" and "Rules Glossary" explain which ability modifiers to use for various D20 Tests.
- **Your Proficiency Bonus If Relevant.** Each creature has a Proficiency Bonus, a number added when making a D20 Test that uses something, such as a skill, in which the creature has proficiency. See "Proficiency" later in "Playing the Game."
- **Circumstantial Bonuses and Penalties.** A class feature, a spell, or another rule might give a bonus or penalty to the die roll.  
**6: Compare the Total to a Target Number.** If the total of the d20 and its modifiers equals or exceeds the target number, the D20 Test succeeds. Otherwise, it fails. The Game Master determines target numbers and tells players whether their rolls are successful. The target number for an ability check or a saving throw is called a Difficulty Class (DC). The target number for an attack roll is called an Armor Class (AC), which appears on a character sheet or in a stat block (see "Rules Glossary").

#### D20 Test  
D20 Tests encompass the three main d20 rolls of the game: ability checks, attack rolls, and saving throws. If something in the game affects D20 Tests, it affects all three of these rolls. The GM determines whether a D20 Test is warranted in a given circumstance. _See also_ "Playing the Game" ("D20 Tests").

#### Proficiency Bonus  
Add your Proficiency Bonus to an ability check when the GM determines that a skill or tool proficiency is relevant to the check and you have that proficiency. For example, if a rule refers to a Strength (Acrobatics or Athletics) check, you can add your Proficiency Bonus to the check if you have proficiency in the Acrobatics or Athletics skill. - **Saving Throws:** The Proficiency Bonus is added to a saving throw when the creature is proficient in the relevant saving throw (e.g., Dexterity saving throw against a spell that the creature has proficiency in).
- **Attack Rolls:** The Proficiency Bonus is added to an attack roll when the creature is proficient with the weapon, ammunition, or spell used to make the attack. For instance, a proficient fighter using a longsword adds their Proficiency Bonus to the attack roll.

answer:
### Comparison of Cackle Fever and Sight Rot

#### Effects
- **Cackle Fever**: Causes 1 Exhaustion level and uncontrollable laughter (Incapacitated condition and Psychic damage on failed Constitution saving throw when taking damage).
- **Sight Rot**: Causes the Blinded condition.

#### Methods of Transmission
- **Cackle Fever**: Transmitted through a 10-foot Emanation around an infected creature to Humanoids (except gnomes).
- **Sight Rot**: Transmitted through drinking tainted water or skin contact with an infected creature to Beasts and Humanoids.

#### Fighting the Contagion
- **Cackle Fever**: Ends after three successful DC 13 Constitution saving throws at the end of each Long Rest. Grants immunity for 1 year.
- **Sight Rot**: Can be ended by _Heal_ or _Lesser Restoration_ spells. Nonmagical ointment (created with an Herbalism Kit) can suppress the contagion for 24 hours; three doses (72 hours total) end the contagion.
question: Compare the effects, methods of transmission, and ways to fight the contagions of Cackle Fever and Sight Rot.

retrieved_context.text:
#### Cackle Fever  
_Magical Contagion_  
Cheaply made potions and elixirs are sometimes tainted by Cackle Fever, which affects Humanoids only (gnomes are strangely immune). A creature suffers the following effects 1d4 days after infection:  
**Fever.** The creature gains 1 Exhaustion level, which lasts until the contagion ends on the creature.  
**Uncontrollable Laughter.** While the creature has the Exhaustion condition, the creature makes a DC 13 Constitution saving throw each time it takes damage other than Psychic damage. On a failed save, the creature takes 5 (1d10) Psychic damage and has the Incapacitated condition as it laughs uncontrollably. At the end of each of its turns, the creature repeats the save, ending the effect on itself on a success. After 1 minute, it succeeds automatically.  
_Fighting the Contagion._ At the end of each Long Rest, an infected creature makes a DC 13 Constitution saving throw. After the creature succeeds on three of these saves, the contagion ends on it, and the creature is immune to Cackle Fever for 1 year.  
_Spreading the Contagion._ Any Humanoid (other than a gnome) that starts its turn within a 10-foot Emanation originating from a creature infected with Cackle Fever must succeed on a DC 10 Constitution saving throw or also become infected with the contagion. On a successful save, the Humanoid can't catch the contagion from that particular infected creature for the next 24 hours.

#### Sight Rot  
_Magical Contagion_  
Any Beast or Humanoid that drinks water tainted by Sight Rot must succeed on a DC 15 Constitution saving throw or have the Blinded condition until the contagion ends.  
_Fighting the Contagion._ Magic such as a _Heal_ or _Lesser Restoration_ spell ends the contagion immediately. A character who is proficient with an Herbalism Kit can use it to create one dose of nonmagical ointment, which takes 1 hour. When applied to the eyes of a creature suffering from Sight Rot, the ointment suppresses the contagion on that creature for 24 hours. If the contagion is suppressed in this way for a total of 72 hours (requiring three doses and applications of the ointment), the contagion ends on the creature.  
_Spreading the Contagion._ Any Humanoid that makes skin contact with a creature infected with Sight Rot must succeed on a DC 15 Constitution saving throw or also become infected with the contagion. On a successful save, the Humanoid can't catch the contagion from that particular infected creature for the next 24 hours.

#### Example Contagions  
The following examples show how magical contagions can work. Feel free to alter the saving throw DCs, effects, and other characteristics of these contagions to suit your campaign.

#### Sewer Plague  
_Magical Contagion_  
Fouled potions and alchemical waste can give rise to Sewer Plague, which incubates in sewers and refuse heaps and is sometimes transmitted by creatures that dwell in such areas, including otyughs and rats. Any Humanoid that is wounded by a creature that carries the contagion or that comes into contact with contaminated filth or offal must succeed on a DC 11 Constitution saving throw or become infected with Sewer Plague. A creature suffers the following effects 1d4 days after infection:  
**Fatigue.** The creature gains 1 Exhaustion level.  
**Weakness.** While the creature has any Exhaustion levels, it regains only half the normal number of Hit Points from spending Hit Point Dice.  
**Restlessness.** While the creature has any Exhaustion levels, finishing a Long Rest neither restores lost Hit Points nor reduces the creature's Exhaustion level.  
_Fighting the Contagion._ Daily at dawn, an infected creature makes a DC 11 Constitution saving throw. On a failed save, the creature gains 1 Exhaustion level as its fatigue worsens. On a successful save, the creature's Exhaustion level decreases by 1. If the creature's Exhaustion level is reduced to 0, the contagion ends on the creature.

#### Contagion  
_Level 5 Necromancy (Cleric, Druid)_  
**Casting Time:** Action
**Range:** Touch
**Component:** V, S
**Duration:** 7 days  
Your touch inflicts a magical contagion. The target must succeed on a Constitution saving throw or take 11d8 Necrotic damage and have the Poisoned condition. Also, choose one ability when you cast the spell. While Poisoned, the target has Disadvantage on saving throws made with the chosen ability.  
The target must repeat the saving throw at the end of each of its turns until it gets three successes or failures. If the target succeeds on three of these saves, the spell ends on the target. If the target fails three of the saves, the spell lasts for 7 days on it.  
Whenever the Poisoned target receives an effect that would end the Poisoned condition, the target must succeed on a Constitution saving throw, or the Poisoned condition doesn't end on it.

## Curses and Magical Contagions  
A curse is a magical burden that lasts for a specified time or until it is ended by some means. A magical contagion is an adverse effect of magical origin that is contagious by definition.  
The following sections discuss curses and magical contagions in detail.

# Cackle Fever vs. Sight Rot: A Comparison

## Effects

**Cackle Fever** affects Humanoids only (with gnomes immune) and has a 1d4 day incubation period. Its effects are twofold:
- **Fever:** The creature gains 1 Exhaustion level that persists until the contagion ends.
- **Uncontrollable Laughter:** While the creature has Exhaustion, each time it takes non-Psychic damage, it must make a DC 13 Constitution save or take 5 (1d10) Psychic damage and become Incapacitated from laughing. This repeats at the end of each turn until the creature succeeds or 1 minute passes.

**Sight Rot** affects Beasts and Humanoids with no incubation period. Its sole effect is:
- **Blinded condition** that lasts until the contagion ends.

## Methods of Transmission

**Cackle Fever** spreads through proximity. Any Humanoid (non-gnome) that starts its turn within a 10-foot emanation of an infected creature must succeed on a DC 10 Constitution save or become infected. A successful save grants 24-hour immunity from that particular infected creature.

**Sight Rot** spreads through contact or tainted water. Any Beast or Humanoid that drinks water tainted by Sight Rot must make a DC 15 Constitution save or become infected. Additionally, any Humanoid making skin contact with an infected creature must make a DC 15 Constitution save or become infected. A successful save grants 24-hour immunity from that particular infected creature.

## Fighting the Contagion

**Cackle Fever** is fought through the body's natural resilience. At the end of each Long Rest, the infected creature makes a DC 13 Constitution save. After three successes, the contagion ends and the creature gains 1-year immunity.

**Sight Rot** requires external intervention:
- **Magic:** A *Heal* or *Lesser Restoration* spell ends it immediately.
- **Herbalism Kit:** A character proficient with an Herbalism Kit can create a nonmagical ointment (1 dose per hour). Applied to the eyes, it suppresses the contagion for 24 hours. After 72 total hours of suppression (3 doses/applications), the contagion ends.

## Summary

Cackle Fever is a proximity-based contagion that causes Exhaustion and debilitating Psychic damage/Incapacitation, resolved through repeated Constitution saves over Long Rests. Sight Rot is a contact/waterborne contagion that causes Blindness, resolved either by magic or by sustained herbal treatment. Cackle Fever has a lower transmission DC (10 vs. 15) but Sight Rot can affect Beasts as well as Humanoids.

Based on the provided SRD 5.2.1 context, here is the comparison between Cackle Fever and Sight Rot:

**Effects**
*   **Cackle Fever:** Affects only Humanoids (gnomes are strangely immune). Symptoms begin 1d4 days after infection. It inflicts 1 level of Exhaustion. While Exhausted, taking any damage other than Psychic damage forces a DC 13 Constitution saving throw. On a failure, the creature takes 1d10 Psychic damage and gains the Incapacitated condition as it laughs uncontrollably. This laughter ends on a successful save at the end of the creature's turn, or automatically after 1 minute.
*   **Sight Rot:** Affects Beasts and Humanoids. It immediately inflicts the Blinded condition upon infection (no incubation period).

**Methods of Transmission**
*   **Cackle Fever:** Initially contracted from cheaply made, tainted potions and elixirs. It spreads when a Humanoid (other than a gnome) starts its turn within a 10-foot Emanation of an infected creature, requiring a DC 10 Constitution saving throw.
*   **Sight Rot:** Initially contracted by drinking tainted water, requiring a DC 15 Constitution saving throw. It spreads when a Humanoid makes skin contact with an infected creature, requiring a DC 15 Constitution saving throw.
*   *Shared Spreading Rule:* For both contagions, succeeding on the saving throw to resist spreading means the creature cannot catch the contagion from that specific infected creature for the next 24 hours.

**Ways to Fight the Contagion**
*   **Cackle Fever:** Fought through natural recovery. The infected creature makes a DC 13 Constitution saving throw at the end of each Long Rest. After three successful saves, the contagion ends, and the creature becomes immune to Cackle Fever for 1 year.
*   **Sight Rot:** Can be fought with magic or medicine. Magic such as the *Heal* or *Lesser Restoration* spell ends it immediately. Nonmagically, a character proficient with an Herbalism Kit can spend 1 hour to create a dose of ointment. Applying it to the eyes suppresses the contagion for 24 hours. If suppressed for a total of 72 hours (three doses/applications), the contagion ends completely.

#### Cackle Fever  
_Magical Contagion_  
Cheaply made potions and elixirs are sometimes tainted by Cackle Fever, which affects Humanoids only (gnomes are strangely immune). A creature suffers the following effects 1d4 days after infection:  
**Fever.** The creature gains 1 Exhaustion level, which lasts until the contagion ends on the creature.  
**Uncontrollable Laughter.** While the creature has the Exhaustion condition, the creature makes a DC 13 Constitution saving throw each time it takes damage other than Psychic damage. On a failed save, the creature takes 5 (1d10) Psychic damage and has the Incapacitated condition as it laughs uncontrollably. At the end of each of its turns, the creature repeats the save, ending the effect on itself on a success. After 1 minute, it succeeds automatically.  
_Fighting the Contagion._ At the end of each Long Rest, an infected creature makes a DC 13 Constitution saving throw. After the creature succeeds on three of these saves, the contagion ends on it, and the creature is immune to Cackle Fever for 1 year.  
_Spreading the Contagion._ Any Humanoid (other than a gnome) that starts its turn within a 10-foot Emanation originating from a creature infected with Cackle Fever must succeed on a DC 10 Constitution saving throw or also become infected with the contagion. On a successful save, the Humanoid can't catch the contagion from that particular infected creature for the next 24 hours.

#### Sight Rot  
_Magical Contagion_  
Any Beast or Humanoid that drinks water tainted by Sight Rot must succeed on a DC 15 Constitution saving throw or have the Blinded condition until the contagion ends.  
_Fighting the Contagion._ Magic such as a _Heal_ or _Lesser Restoration_ spell ends the contagion immediately. A character who is proficient with an Herbalism Kit can use it to create one dose of nonmagical ointment, which takes 1 hour. When applied to the eyes of a creature suffering from Sight Rot, the ointment suppresses the contagion on that creature for 24 hours. If the contagion is suppressed in this way for a total of 72 hours (requiring three doses and applications of the ointment), the contagion ends on the creature.  
_Spreading the Contagion._ Any Humanoid that makes skin contact with a creature infected with Sight Rot must succeed on a DC 15 Constitution saving throw or also become infected with the contagion. On a successful save, the Humanoid can't catch the contagion from that particular infected creature for the next 24 hours.

#### Example Contagions  
The following examples show how magical contagions can work. Feel free to alter the saving throw DCs, effects, and other characteristics of these contagions to suit your campaign.

#### Sewer Plague  
_Magical Contagion_  
Fouled potions and alchemical waste can give rise to Sewer Plague, which incubates in sewers and refuse heaps and is sometimes transmitted by creatures that dwell in such areas, including otyughs and rats. Any Humanoid that is wounded by a creature that carries the contagion or that comes into contact with contaminated filth or offal must succeed on a DC 11 Constitution saving throw or become infected with Sewer Plague. A creature suffers the following effects 1d4 days after infection:  
**Fatigue.** The creature gains 1 Exhaustion level.  
**Weakness.** While the creature has any Exhaustion levels, it regains only half the normal number of Hit Points from spending Hit Point Dice.  
**Restlessness.** While the creature has any Exhaustion levels, finishing a Long Rest neither restores lost Hit Points nor reduces the creature's Exhaustion level.  
_Fighting the Contagion._ Daily at dawn, an infected creature makes a DC 11 Constitution saving throw. On a failed save, the creature gains 1 Exhaustion level as its fatigue worsens. On a successful save, the creature's Exhaustion level decreases by 1. If the creature's Exhaustion level is reduced to 0, the contagion ends on the creature.

#### Contagion  
_Level 5 Necromancy (Cleric, Druid)_  
**Casting Time:** Action
**Range:** Touch
**Component:** V, S
**Duration:** 7 days  
Your touch inflicts a magical contagion. The target must succeed on a Constitution saving throw or take 11d8 Necrotic damage and have the Poisoned condition. Also, choose one ability when you cast the spell. While Poisoned, the target has Disadvantage on saving throws made with the chosen ability.  
The target must repeat the saving throw at the end of each of its turns until it gets three successes or failures. If the target succeeds on three of these saves, the spell ends on the target. If the target fails three of the saves, the spell lasts for 7 days on it.  
Whenever the Poisoned target receives an effect that would end the Poisoned condition, the target must succeed on a Constitution saving throw, or the Poisoned condition doesn't end on it.

## Curses and Magical Contagions  
A curse is a magical burden that lasts for a specified time or until it is ended by some means. A magical contagion is an adverse effect of magical origin that is contagious by definition.

**Narrative Curse vs. Environmental Curse**

- **Narrative Curse**  
  - **Origin:** Imposed by the story or the DM as a consequence of a specific taboo, violation, or moral transgression (e.g., breaking a vow, defiling a sacred site, murdering an innocent).  
  - **Purpose:** Serves the plot, providing a clear reason for the curse and often a path to redemption (e.g., the character must right the wrong to lift it).  
  - **Mechanics:** The effects are defined by the DM and can be tailored to fit the adventure’s theme. A spell like *Remove Curse* might only suppress the curse temporarily, leaving the underlying narrative consequence intact.  
  - **Example:** A character who desecrates a tomb might be cursed to suffer misfortune until they restore the tomb’s honor.

- **Environmental Curse**  
  - **Origin:** Tied to a location or condition that is inherently infused with negative energy or evil (e.g., a desecrated site, a place haunted by demonic spirits).  
  - **Purpose:** Creates a persistent, location‑based hazard that affects anyone who remains within its influence, often reflecting the setting’s lore (e.g., the chaotic nature of the Abyss).  
  - **Mechanics:** The curse is automatically triggered by exposure to the environment and follows the rules set for that specific curse. It can be removed by spells that dispel curses or by completing the environmental challenge (e.g., leaving the area, performing a ritual).  
  - **Example:** **Demonic Possession** – a creature that lingers in a desecrated, Abyss‑tainted location must succeed on a DC 15 Charisma saving throw or be possessed by a bodiless demonic entity. The possession persists until the creature makes a saving throw at the end of each turn, finishes a Long Rest and succeeds on a saving throw, or is affected by *Dispel Evil and Good* or a similar curse‑removing effect.

**Key Differences Illustrated by Demonic Possession (Environmental Curse):**  
- **Trigger:** Environmental (exposure to a cursed location) rather than a narrative act.  
- **Mechanics:** Automatic possession on failure, with specific roll‑based control mechanics and removal conditions tied to the environment.  
- **Narrative Role:** Reflects the setting’s evil atmosphere; the curse is a hazard of the place, not a punishment for a specific moral lapse.

In contrast, a **Narrative Curse** would be imposed for a character’s specific wrongdoing (e.g., breaking a sacred oath) and would be tied to that act, with its removal linked to rectifying the act, rather than simply leaving a cursed location.

A creature affected by such a curse should know why they're being punished and be able to learn how to end their curse, likely by symbolically righting the wrong they committed. A curse is a magical burden that lasts for a specified time or until it is ended by some means. A magical contagion is an adverse effect of magical origin that is contagious by definition.

### Curses  
A curse typically takes one of the forms detailed below.

#### Cursed Creatures  
Some monsters are associated with curses, whether as part of their origins or due to their ability to spread curses—werewolves being a prime example.  
You decide how a spell like _Remove Curse_ affects a creature with accursed origins. For example, you might decide that a mummy was created through a curse and it can be destroyed permanently only by casting _Remove Curse_ on its corpse.

#### Curses  
Some game effects curse a creature or an object. The effect that confers a curse defines what the curse does. Curses can be removed by the _Remove Curse_ and _Greater Restoration_ spells or other magic that explicitly ends curses.

When multiple spells overlap in their effects, the rules state that the effects of different spells **add together** while their durations overlap (Combining Spell Effects). This means that if two distinct spells with different effects are active on the same target at the same time, their effects are combined.

However, if the **same spell** is cast multiple times on the same target, the effects do **not** combine. Instead, the most potent effect applies while the durations overlap. The specific rule is:

- **Most Potent Effect:** For equally potent castings of the same spell, the most recent casting's effect applies.
- **Example:** If two clerics cast **Bless** on the same target, the target gains the benefit only once (no double bonus dice). If the durations overlap, the effect continues until the second **Bless** ends.

Thus, overlapping effects from different spells are combined, while overlapping effects from the same spell are resolved by taking the most potent (or most recent) effect.

## Combining Spell Effects  
The effects of different spells add together while their durations overlap. In contrast, the effects of the same spell cast multiple times don't combine. Instead, the most potent effect—such as the highest bonus—from those castings applies while their durations overlap. The most recent effect applies if the castings are equally potent and their durations overlap. For example, if two Clerics cast _Bless_ on the same target, that target gains the spell's benefit only once; the target doesn't receive two bonus dice. But if the durations of the spells overlap, the effect continues until the duration of the second _Bless_ ends.  
> **IDENTIFYING AN ONGOING SPELL**
>
> You can try to identify a non-instantaneous spell by its observable effects if its duration is ongoing. To identify it, you must take the Study action and succeed on a DC 15 Intelligence (Arcana) check.

## Effects  
The effects of a spell are detailed after its duration entry. Those details present exactly what the spell does, which ignores mundane physical laws; any outcomes beyond those effects are under the GM's purview. Whatever the effects, they typically deal with targets, saving throws, attack rolls, or all three, each of which is detailed below.

#### Damage against Multiple Targets  
When you create a damaging effect that forces two or more targets to make saving throws against it at the same time, roll the damage once for all the targets. For example, when a wizard casts _Fireball_, the spell's damage is rolled once for all creatures caught in the blast.

## Targets  
A typical spell requires the caster to pick one or more targets to be affected by the spell's magic. A spell's description says whether the spell targets creatures, objects, or something else.  
_A Clear Path to the Target._ To target something with a spell, a caster must have a clear path to it, so it can't be behind Total Cover.  
_Targeting Yourself._ If a spell targets a creature of your choice, you can choose yourself unless the creature must be Hostile or specifically a creature other than you.  
_Areas of Effect._ Some spells, such as _Thunderwave_, cover an area called an area of effect, which is defined in "Rules Glossary." The area determines what the spell targets. The description of a spell specifies whether it has an area of effect, which is typically one of these shapes: Cone, Cube, Cylinder, Emanation, Line, or Sphere.

answer:
Based on the provided rules, here are the differences between an Environmental Curse and a Narrative Curse:

**Origin and Trigger**
* **Environmental Curses** are hazards tied to specific places or items. They burden creatures who linger in evil or desecrated locations, or who interact with specific objects. 
* **Narrative Curses** are supernatural punishments triggered by a creature's actions, specifically the violation of a taboo (such as breaking a vow, defiling a tomb, or murdering an innocent).

**Mechanics and Effects**
* **Environmental Curses** have specific, defined mechanical rules. **Demonic Possession** is a prime example: arising from the chaos of the Abyss, it forces a creature to make a DC 15 Charisma saving throw to avoid being possessed by a bodiless demonic entity. If possessed, the demon takes control whenever the victim rolls a 1 on a D20 Test. The victim can attempt a DC 15 Charisma save at the end of each of their later turns to temporarily regain control, or make a save after a Long Rest to end the effect.
* **Narrative Curses** do not have predefined mechanics. Their effects are entirely designed or customized by the DM to fit the story, and they should feel like rare, potent magic rooted in the campaign's lore.

**Awareness and Resolution**
* **Environmental Curses** are typically resolved through mechanical means, such as succeeding on saving throws, resting, or using standard curse-removing magic. For instance, Demonic Possession is explicitly ended by a *Dispel Evil and Good* spell or any magic that removes a curse.
* **Narrative Curses** require narrative resolution. The affected creature should know *why* they are being punished and *how* to end it, usually by symbolically righting the wrong they committed. Furthermore, standard magic like *Remove Curse* might not permanently cure a narrative curse; the DM decides how the spell interacts with it, and it might merely suppress the curse's effects for a time.
question: Explain the differences between a Narrative Curse and an Environmental Curse, using Demonic Possession as a specific example for the latter.

retrieved_context.text:
#### Environmental Curses  
Some locations are so suffused with evil that anyone who lingers there is burdened with a curse. Demonic Possession is one example of an environmental curse.  
_Demonic Possession._ Demonic Possession arises from the chaos and evil of the Abyss and commonly besets creatures that interact with demonic objects or linger in desecrated locations, where demonic spirits await victims.  
A creature that becomes the target of Demonic Possession must succeed on a DC 15 Charisma saving throw or be possessed by a bodiless demonic entity. Whenever the possessed creature rolls a 1 on a D20 Test, the demonic entity takes control of the creature and determines the creature's behavior thereafter. At the end of each of the possessed creature's later turns, the creature makes a DC 15 Charisma saving throw, regaining control of itself on a success.  
After finishing a Long Rest, a creature with Demonic Possession makes a DC 15 Charisma saving throw. On a successful save, the effect ends on the creature. A _Dispel Evil and Good_ spell or any magic that removes a curse also ends the effect on it.

#### Narrative Curses  
A curse might manifest during an adventure when a creature's violation of a taboo warrants supernatural punishment, such as breaking a vow, defiling a tomb, or murdering an innocent. Such a curse can have any effects you design, or it might be a customized version of another type of curse discussed in this section.  
A creature affected by such a curse should know why they're being punished and be able to learn how to end their curse, likely by symbolically righting the wrong they committed. How a spell like _Remove Curse_ affects a curse that's part of your adventure is up to you—the spell might merely suppress the effects of the curse for a time. Regardless, narrative curses should feel like rare, potent magic rooted in the lore of your campaign.

## Curses and Magical Contagions  
A curse is a magical burden that lasts for a specified time or until it is ended by some means. A magical contagion is an adverse effect of magical origin that is contagious by definition.  
The following sections discuss curses and magical contagions in detail.

### Curses  
A curse typically takes one of the forms detailed below.

#### Cursed Creatures  
Some monsters are associated with curses, whether as part of their origins or due to their ability to spread curses—werewolves being a prime example.  
You decide how a spell like _Remove Curse_ affects a creature with accursed origins. For example, you might decide that a mummy was created through a curse and it can be destroyed permanently only by casting _Remove Curse_ on its corpse.

#### Curses  
Some game effects curse a creature or an object. The effect that confers a curse defines what the curse does. Curses can be removed by the _Remove Curse_ and _Greater Restoration_ spells or other magic that explicitly ends curses.

Based on the SRD 5.2.1 rules, here is how overlapping spell effects are handled:

**Combining Different Spells:** The effects of different spells add together while their durations overlap.

**Combining the Same Spell:** The effects of the same spell cast multiple times don't combine. Instead:

## Combining Spell Effects  
The effects of different spells add together while their durations overlap. In contrast, the effects of the same spell cast multiple times don't combine. Instead, the most potent effect—such as the highest bonus—from those castings applies while their durations overlap. The most recent effect applies if the castings are equally potent and their durations overlap. For example, if two Clerics cast _Bless_ on the same target, that target gains the spell's benefit only once; the target doesn't receive two bonus dice. But if the durations of the spells overlap, the effect continues until the duration of the second _Bless_ ends.  
> **IDENTIFYING AN ONGOING SPELL**
>
> You can try to identify a non-instantaneous spell by its observable effects if its duration is ongoing. To identify it, you must take the Study action and succeed on a DC 15 Intelligence (Arcana) check.

## Effects  
The effects of a spell are detailed after its duration entry. Those details present exactly what the spell does, which ignores mundane physical laws; any outcomes beyond those effects are under the GM's purview. Whatever the effects, they typically deal with targets, saving throws, attack rolls, or all three, each of which is detailed below.

#### Damage against Multiple Targets  
When you create a damaging effect that forces two or more targets to make saving throws against it at the same time, roll the damage once for all the targets. For example, when a wizard casts _Fireball_, the spell's damage is rolled once for all creatures caught in the blast.

## Targets  
A typical spell requires the caster to pick one or more targets to be affected by the spell's magic. A spell's description says whether the spell targets creatures, objects, or something else.  
_A Clear Path to the Target._ To target something with a spell, a caster must have a clear path to it, so it can't be behind Total Cover.  
_Targeting Yourself._ If a spell targets a creature of your choice, you can choose yourself unless the creature must be Hostile or specifically a creature other than you.  
_Areas of Effect._ Some spells, such as _Thunderwave_, cover an area called an area of effect, which is defined in "Rules Glossary." The area determines what the spell targets. The description of a spell specifies whether it has an area of effect, which is typically one of these shapes: Cone, Cube, Cylinder, Emanation, Line, or Sphere.  
_Awareness of Being Targeted._ Unless a spell has a perceptible effect, a creature doesn't know it was targeted by the spell. An effect like lightning is obvious, but a more subtle effect, such as an attempt to read thoughts, goes unnoticed unless a spell's description says otherwise.  
_Invalid Targets._ If you cast a spell on someone or something that can't be affected by it, nothing happens to that target, but if you used a spell slot to cast the spell, the slot is still expended.  
If the spell normally has no effect on a target that succeeds on a saving throw, the invalid target appears to have succeeded on its saving throw, even though it didn't attempt one (giving no hint that the creature is an invalid target). Otherwise, you perceive that the spell did nothing to the target.

#### Simultaneous Effects  
If two or more things happen at the same time on a turn, the person at the game table—player or GM—whose turn it is decides the order in which those things happen. For example, if two effects occur at the start of a player character's turn, the player decides which of the effects happens first.

**Fast Hands (Thief Rogue, Level 3)**  
- **Cost:** No resource cost; it is a class feature that can be used as a **Bonus Action**.  
- **Effect:** As a Bonus Action you may either (a) make a Dexterity (Sleight of Hand) check to pick a lock or disarm a trap with Thieves’ Tools, or (b) take the **Utilize** action (or the **Magic** action for a magic item that requires it).  
- **Limitations:**  
  - It can be used **once per turn** (the Bonus Action slot).  
  - It only applies to the listed activities (lock‑picking, trap disarming, or using a magic item via Utilize/Magic).  
  - It does **not** affect spell casting or other actions beyond those specified.  

**Quickened Spell (Sorcerer Metamagic, Level 2)**  
- **Cost:** **2 Sorcery Points** per use.  
- **Effect:** When you cast a spell whose casting time is **an Action**, you may spend 2 Sorcery Points to change that casting time to a **Bonus Action** for that casting.  
- **Limitations:**  
  - You cannot modify a spell in this way if you have already **cast a level‑1+ spell on the current turn** (i.e., you cannot Quickened‑cast after another spell of 1st level or higher has been cast that turn).  
  - After Quickening a spell, you cannot cast another level‑1+ spell on the same turn.  
  - Only **one** Metamagic option can be applied to a single spell; Quickened is the sole option described here.  

**Key Differences**  
1. **Resource Requirement** – Fast Hands costs **no resource**; Quickened Spell costs **2 Sorcery Points**.  
2. **Scope of Action** – Fast Hands lets you perform **specific non‑spell actions** (lock‑picking, trap disarming, or using a magic item) as a Bonus Action. Quickened Spell **reduces the casting time of any spell** (that has an Action casting time) to a Bonus Action.  
3. **Turn‑based Restrictions** – Fast Hands is unrestricted beyond the single Bonus Action per turn. Quickened Spell is limited by the **“no other level‑1+ spell this turn”** rule and by the need to have Sorcery Points available.  
4. **Applicability** – Fast Hands applies only to **sleight‑of‑hand or item‑use** activities; Quickened Spell applies to **any spell** with an Action casting time.  

In summary, both features let a character act more efficiently by using a Bonus Action, but Fast Hands is a free, class‑specific utility for rogue‑type tasks, while Quickened Spell is a paid metamagic option that reshapes spell casting at the cost of Sorcery Points and with specific turn‑order constraints.

A level 1 spell fits into a slot of any size, but a level 2 spell fits only into a slot that's at least level 2. To determine the number of spell slots for a character who has taken **one level in every spellcasting class** available in the SRD 5.2.1, we follow the **Multiclass Spellcaster** rules.

### Step 1: Identify all spellcasting classes in the SRD 5.2.1
From the SRD 5.2.1, the classes that grant the **Spellcasting** feature at level 1 are:
- Bard  
- Cleric  
- Druid  
- Sorcerer  
- Wizard  
- Ranger  
- Paladin  

The Warlock is **not** included in the Spellcasting feature calculation because it uses **Pact Magic**, which is handled separately (though Pact Magic slots can be used interchangeably with Spellcasting slots, they are **not added** to the multiclass spell slot total).

So we have **7 classes** that provide Spellcasting (including Ranger and Paladin).

### Step 2: Apply multiclass spell slot rules
Per the SRD:

> - All your levels in the **Bard, Cleric, Druid, Sorcerer, and Wizard** classes  
> - **Half your levels (round up)** in the **Paladin and Ranger** classes  

The character has **1 level** in each of these classes:

- Full-caster levels: Bard 1 + Cleric 1 + Druid 1 + Sorcerer 1 + Wizard 1 = **5 levels**  
- Half-caster levels: Paladin 1 + Ranger 1 → each contributes **½ level, rounded up** → 1 + 1 = **2 levels**

> **Total effective level for spell slots = 5 + 2 = 7**

### Step 3: Look up spell slots for level 7 in the Multiclass Spellcaster table

From the table:

- Level 7 gives:  
  - **4** 1st-level slots  
  - **3** 2nd-level slots  
  - **3** 3rd-level slots  
  - Higher-level slots: **none**

### Final Answer:
A character with **one level in each spellcasting class** (Bard, Cleric, Druid, Sorcerer, Wizard, Paladin, Ranger) has **4 first-level, 3 second-level, and 3 third-level spell slots**.

> **Total spell slots = 10**, distributed as above.

Note: Warlock is excluded from this calculation because Pact Magic is not added to the multiclass spell slot total (though its slots can be used to cast spells from other classes, and vice versa). The SRD 5.2.1 does not list Warlock as part of the Spellcasting feature group for multiclass slot calculation.

You determine what spells you can prepare for each class individually, as if you were a single-classed member of that class. If you are a level 4 Ranger / level 3 Sorcerer, for example, you can prepare five level 1 Ranger spells, and you can prepare six Sorcerer spells of level 1 or 2 (as well as four Sorcerer cantrips). Each spell you prepare is associated with one of your classes, and you use the spellcasting ability of that class when you cast the spell. _Cantrips_. If a cantrip of yours increases in power at higher levels, the increase is based on your total character level, not your level in a particular class, unless the spell says otherwise. _Spell Slots_. You use the slots for that level to cast spells of an appropriate level from any class whose Spellcasting feature you have. This table might give you spell slots of a higher level than the spells you prepare. You can use those slots but only to cast your lower-level spells. If a lower-level spell that you cast, like _Burning Hands_, has an enhanced effect when cast at a higher level, you can use the enhanced effect as normal. #### Spell Slots  
Spellcasting is taxing, so a spellcaster can cast only a limited number of level 1+ spells before resting. Spell slots are the main way a spellcaster's magical potential is represented. Each spellcasting class gives its members a limited number of spell slots of certain spell levels. For example, a level 3 Wizard has four level 1 spell slots and two level 2 slots.  
When you cast a spell, you expend a slot of that spell's level or higher, effectively "filling" a slot with the spell. Imagine a spell slot is a groove of a certain size—small for a level 1 slot and larger for a higher-level spell. A level 1 spell fits into a slot of any size, but a level 2 spell fits only into a slot that's at least level 2. So when a level 3 Wizard casts _Magic Missile_, a level 1 spell, that Wizard spends one of four level 1 slots and has three remaining.  
Finishing a Long Rest restores any expended spell slots.

#### As a Multiclass Character  
- Gain the following traits from the Core Ranger Traits table: Hit Point Die, proficiency with Martial weapons, proficiency in one skill of your choice from the Ranger's skill list, and training with Light and Medium armor and Shields.
- Gain the Ranger's level 1 features, which are listed in the Ranger Features table. See the multiclassing rules in "Character Creation" to determine your available spell slots.

## Multiclassing  
Multiclassing allows you to gain levels in multiple classes. With this rule, you have the option of gaining a level in a new class whenever you advance in level instead of gaining a level in your current class. Doing so lets you mix the abilities of those classes to realize a character concept that might not be reflected in a single class.

#### As a Multiclass Character  
• Gain the following traits from the Core Druid Traits table: Hit Point Die and training with Light armor and Shields.
• Gain the Druid's level 1 features, which are listed in the Druid Features table. See the multiclassing rules in "Character Creation" to determine your available spell slots.

#### Level 18: Spell Mastery  
You have achieved such mastery over certain spells that you can cast them at will. Choose a level 1 and a level 2 spell in your spellbook that have a casting time of an action. You always have those spells prepared, and you can cast them at their lowest level without expending a spell slot. To cast either spell at a higher level, you must expend a spell slot.  
Whenever you finish a Long Rest, you can study your spellbook and replace one of those spells with an eligible spell of the same level from the book.

A player can recover spell slots without using a Long Rest through the following class features that allow spell slot recovery after a Short Rest:

1. **Druid (Level 6: Natural Recovery)** – When a Druid finishes a Short Rest, they may choose expended spell slots to recover, provided the combined level of the recovered slots does not exceed half the Druid's level (rounded up). The recovered slots cannot be level 6 or higher. This recovery is usable once per Short Rest and requires a subsequent Long Rest before it can be used again.

2. **Wizard (Level 1: Arcane Recovery)** – A Wizard can regain spell slots by studying their spellbook after finishing a Short Rest. The combined level of the recovered slots must be no more than half the Wizard's level (rounded up), and none of the slots can be level 6 or higher. This feature can be used once per Short Rest, with a Long Rest required before it can be used again.

3. **Pact Magic User (Level 2: Magical Cunning)** – This feature allows a character to regain expended Pact Magic spell slots after performing a 1‑minute esoteric rite at the end of a Short Rest. The number of slots regained cannot exceed half the character's maximum spell slots (rounded up). This can be used once per Short Rest, requiring a Long Rest before it can be used again.

These are the only mechanisms within the provided SRD 5.2.1 context that allow spell slot recovery without a Long Rest. Other class features, such as Sorcerous Restoration or Spell Mastery, do not directly recover spell slots but instead provide alternative means of spellcasting or spell substitution.

retrieved_context.text:
#### Level 6: Natural Recovery  
You can cast one of the level 1+ spells that you have prepared from your Circle Spells feature without expending a spell slot, and you must finish a Long Rest before you do so again.  
In addition, when you finish a Short Rest, you can choose expended spell slots to recover. The spell slots can have a combined level that is equal to or less than half your Druid level (round up), and none of them can be level 6+. For example, if you're a level 6 Druid, you can recover up to three levels' worth of spell slots. You can recover a level 3 spell slot, a level 2 and a level 1 spell slot, or three level 1 spell slots. Once you recover spell slots with this feature, you can't do so again until you finish a Long Rest.

#### Level 1: Arcane Recovery  
You can regain some of your magical energy by studying your spellbook. When you finish a Short Rest, you can choose expended spell slots to recover. The spell slots can have a combined level equal to no more than half your Wizard level (round up), and none of the slots can be level 6 or higher. For example, if you're a level 4 Wizard, you can recover up to two levels' worth of spell slots, regaining either one level 2 spell slot or two level 1 spell slots.  
Once you use this feature, you can't do so again until you finish a Long Rest.

#### Spell Slots  
Spellcasting is taxing, so a spellcaster can cast only a limited number of level 1+ spells before resting. Spell slots are the main way a spellcaster's magical potential is represented. Each spellcasting class gives its members a limited number of spell slots of certain spell levels. For example, a level 3 Wizard has four level 1 spell slots and two level 2 slots.  
When you cast a spell, you expend a slot of that spell's level or higher, effectively "filling" a slot with the spell. Imagine a spell slot is a groove of a certain size—small for a level 1 slot and larger for a higher-level spell. A level 1 spell fits into a slot of any size, but a level 2 spell fits only into a slot that's at least level 2. So when a level 3 Wizard casts _Magic Missile_, a level 1 spell, that Wizard spends one of four level 1 slots and has three remaining.  
Finishing a Long Rest restores any expended spell slots.

#### Level 5: Sorcerous Restoration  
When you finish a Short Rest, you can regain expended Sorcery Points, but no more than a number equal to half your Sorcerer level (round down). Once you use this feature, you can't do so again until you finish a Long Rest.

#### Level 18: Spell Mastery  
You have achieved such mastery over certain spells that you can cast them at will. Choose a level 1 and a level 2 spell in your spellbook that have a casting time of an action. You always have those spells prepared, and you can cast them at their lowest level without expending a spell slot. To cast either spell at a higher level, you must expend a spell slot.  
Whenever you finish a Long Rest, you can study your spellbook and replace one of those spells with an eligible spell of the same level from the book.

#### Level 2: Magical Cunning  
You can perform an esoteric rite for 1 minute. At the end of it, you regain expended Pact Magic spell slots but no more than a number equal to half your maximum (round up). Once you use this feature, you can't do so again until you finish a Long Rest.

#### Level 6: Natural Recovery  
You can cast one of the level 1+ spells that you have prepared from your Circle Spells feature without expending a spell slot, and you must finish a Long Rest before you do so again.  
In addition, when you finish a Short Rest, you can choose expended spell slots to recover. The spell slots can have a combined level that is equal to or less than half your Druid level (round up), and none of them can be level 6+. For example, if you're a level 6 Druid, you can recover up to three levels' worth of spell slots. You can recover a level 3 spell slot, a level 2 and a level 1 spell slot, or three level 1 spell slots. Once you recover spell slots with this feature, you can't do so again until you finish a Long Rest.

#### Level 1: Arcane Recovery  
You can regain some of your magical energy by studying your spellbook. When you finish a Short Rest, you can choose expended spell slots to recover. The spell slots can have a combined level equal to no more than half your Wizard level (round up), and none of the slots can be level 6 or higher. For example, if you're a level 4 Wizard, you can recover up to two levels' worth of spell slots, regaining either one level 2 spell slot or two level 1 spell slots.  
Once you use this feature, you can't do so again until you finish a Long Rest.

#### Spell Slots  
Spellcasting is taxing, so a spellcaster can cast only a limited number of level 1+ spells before resting. Spell slots are the main way a spellcaster's magical potential is represented. Each spellcasting class gives its members a limited number of spell slots of certain spell levels. For example, a level 3 Wizard has four level 1 spell slots and two level 2 slots.  
When you cast a spell, you expend a slot of that spell's level or higher, effectively "filling" a slot with the spell. Imagine a spell slot is a groove of a certain size—small for a level 1 slot and larger for a higher-level spell. A level 1 spell fits into a slot of any size, but a level 2 spell fits only into a slot that's at least level 2. So when a level 3 Wizard casts _Magic Missile_, a level 1 spell, that Wizard spends one of four level 1 slots and has three remaining.  
Finishing a Long Rest restores any expended spell slots.

#### Level 5: Sorcerous Restoration  
When you finish a Short Rest, you can regain expended Sorcery Points, but no more than a number equal to half your Sorcerer level (round down). Once you use this feature, you can't do so again until you finish a Long Rest.

#### Level 18: Spell Mastery  
You have achieved such mastery over certain spells that you can cast them at will. Choose a level 1 and a level 2 spell in your spellbook that have a casting time of an action. You always have those spells prepared, and you can cast them at their lowest level without expending a spell slot. To cast either spell at a higher level, you must expend a spell slot.  
Whenever you finish a Long Rest, you can study your spellbook and replace one of those spells with an eligible spell of the same level from the book.

#### Level 2: Magical Cunning  
You can perform an esoteric rite for 1 minute. At the end of it, you regain expended Pact Magic spell slots but no more than a number equal to half your maximum (round up). Once you use this feature, you can't do so again until you finish a Long Rest.

# Do You Need Stealth If You're Invisible?

**No, you do not need to take the Hide action to gain the Invisible condition if you become invisible through other means** (such as the *Invisibility* spell, the Warlock's One with Shadows feature, or similar effects).

The Invisible condition and the Hide action are **separate mechanics** that can overlap but are not dependent on each other:

- **The Invisible condition** (source [1]) grants you Concealed status, gives you Advantage on attack rolls, and imposes Disadvantage on attack rolls against you — all without requiring a Stealth check.

- **The Hide action** (source [2]) is one *way* to gain the Invisible condition, but it requires a DC 15 Dexterity (Stealth) check and specific conditions (Heavily Obscured, Three-Quarters Cover, or Total Cover, plus being out of enemies' line of sight).

So if you cast *Invisibility* on yourself, you gain the Invisible condition immediately — no Stealth check needed. You are effectively unseen and unheard (the condition makes you concealed), and you get the associated combat benefits.

**However**, there is a practical reason you might *still* want to Hide even while invisible: the Hide action sets a **DC for enemies to find you** with a Wisdom (Perception) check (source [2]). Without that, enemies may still know your general location and can target the space you're in (they'd just have Disadvantage on the attack roll). Hiding gives you a more concrete "you are undetectable" state with a defined DC to be found.

**In summary:** Invisibility alone does not require Stealth. But combining invisibility with the Hide action gives you additional protection by establishing a Perception DC for enemies to locate you.

### Reactions  
Certain special abilities, spells, and situations allow you to take a special action called a Reaction. A Reaction is an instant response to a trigger of some kind, which can occur on your turn or on someone else's. The Opportunity Attack, described later in "Playing the Game," is the most common type of Reaction.  
When you take a Reaction, you can't take another one until the start of your next turn. If the reaction interrupts another creature's turn, that creature can continue its turn right after the Reaction.  
In terms of timing, a Reaction takes place immediately after its trigger unless the Reaction's description says otherwise.

#### Reaction  
A Reaction is a special action taken in response to a trigger defined in the Reaction's description. You can take a Reaction on another creature's turn, and if you take it on your turn, you can do so even if you also take an action, a Bonus Action, or both. Once you take a Reaction, you can't take another one until the start of your next turn. The Opportunity Attack is a Reaction available to all creatures. _See also_ "Opportunity Attacks" and "Playing the Game" ("Actions").

### Reactions  
If the monster has Reaction options, those are listed in this section along with their triggers. See "Playing the Game" for details on Reactions.

#### Simultaneous Effects  
If two or more things happen at the same time on a turn, the person at the game table—player or GM—whose turn it is decides the order in which those things happen. For example, if two effects occur at the start of a player character's turn, the player decides which of the effects happens first.

#### Action On your turn, you can take one action. Choose which action to take from those below or from the special actions provided by your features. _See also_ "Playing the Game" ("Actions"). These actions are defined elsewhere in this glossary:
Attack Dodge Influence Search
Dash Help Magic Study
Disengage Hide Ready Utilize

#### Ready [Action]  
You take the Ready action to wait for a particular circumstance before you act. To do so, you take this action on your turn, which lets you act by taking a Reaction before the start of your next turn.  
First, you decide what perceivable circumstance will trigger your Reaction. Then, you choose the action you will take in response to that trigger, or you choose to move up to your Speed in response to it. Examples include "If the cultist steps on the
trapdoor, I'll pull the lever that opens it," and "If the zombie steps next to me, I move away."  
When the trigger occurs, you can either take your Reaction right after the trigger finishes or ignore the trigger.  
When you Ready a spell, you cast it as normal (expending any resources used to cast it) but hold its energy, which you release with your Reaction when the trigger occurs. To be readied, a spell must have a casting time of an action, and holding on to the spell's magic requires Concentration, which you can maintain up to the start of your next turn. If your Concentration is broken, the spell dissipates without taking effect.
